I have the honour to communicate the following letter to the House:
Ottawa, Dec. 3, 1909.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that Chief Justice, the Right Hon. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, acting as Deputy Governor General, will proceed to the Senate Chamber this afternoon at 3.15 for the purpose of assenting to a certain Bill which has passed the Senate and the House of Commons during the present session of parliament.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,

Assistant Governor General's Secretary. To the Honourable
The Speaker of the House of Commons.
A message was delivered by Captain J. Ernest Chambers, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, His Honour the Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of your honourable House in the Chamber of the honourable the Senate.	,
Accordingly the House went up to the Senate Chamber.
And the House being returned.
Mr. SPEAKER informed the House that his honour the deputy of His Excellency the Governor General had been pleased to give, in His Majesty's name, the Royal assent to the following Bill:
An Act respecting a certain supplementary convention between His Majesty and the President of the French Republic.

DEMERS (St. John and Iberville) -(Translation)-moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 56) to amend the Bank Act. He said :	These amendments are made
primo, .in order that banking operations may be more known to the shareholders when advances to a considerable amount are made to the bank's customers; second, to make the special general meeting of the shareholders more easy by allowing fifteen amongst them, in possession of one-twentieth of a bank share, to ask for the convocation of such meeting, instead of twenty-five shareholders in possession of one-tenth of these shares, such as prescribed by law; certio, this Bill is designed to get rid of those dishonest or undesirable shareholders; last, the object of the fourth amendment is to- establish a system of banks' inspection through the Department of Finance of Canada.
Bill read first time.

Mr. SAMUEL SHARPE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 57) to amend the Bank Act. He said: This is the same Bill as that which I introduced in the early part of the session with the exception of the clause with regard to the payment of interest. It was suggested to me, that, owing to that clause, if the Bill became law, it might involve a charge upon the consolidated revenue of the country and in consequence would be irregular. It was-suggested that I should secure the discharge of the order and reintroduce the Bill with the omission of that clause. The object of the Bill, as I explained on a former occasion, is to provide that the unclaimed balances at the banks should be transferred to the government who shall become the custodians and trustees thereof.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That when this House adjourns on Tuesday the 7th inst. it stands adjourned until Thursday the 9th.
What is the trouble with Wednesday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Wednesday is a legal holiday by statute-the feast of the Immaculate Conception.

I want to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if there is any correspondence in existence between himself and the two ministers who went over to the conference this summer, or with any member of the British government, concerning the negotiations, business and attitude to be taken by the representatives of Canada, or any letters of instruction or anything of the kind? I had a motion prepared to ask for all the papers and correspondence. I did not push it because these papers that ,we have came down but they do not include anything except that it took place over there. If there is any correspondence, in the nature of instructions, letters or otherwise I think we ought to have that before the discussion on the second reading of the Bill comes on. I am not sure whether there is any or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All the correspondence upon this subject has been brought down. If there had been any correspondence of a confidential nature, of course, it would not have been proper for me to have brought it down, but I can tell my hon. friend that there is not even correspondence of a confidential nature. Everything is before the House.

I would like to ask the government when those papers ordered on the 22nd November will be brought down. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) is not in his place. Perhaps the Prime Minister will call his attention to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will take a note of it.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr Aylesworth) whether he has under consideration a recommendation of further executive clemency in the case of Mrs. Robinson, recently found guilty of murder at the Sudbury assizes and whose sentence was subsequently, upon the petition of upwards of 100,000 Canadian citizens, commuted by His Excellency in Council to imprisonment in the penitentiary of Kingston for ten years. Is it the intention of the Minister of Justice or the government to release Mrs. Robinson on parole or otherwise, or in any other way to effect any further mitigation of the very severe punishment which she is suffering, which will result in her release at any early day?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The case referred to was the subject of very anxious and careful consideration before the date fixed for the execution of the capital sentence with the result that His Excellency was advised to commute the capital sentence into a sentence of imprisonment in the penitentiary for a period of ten years. Since the announcement of the decision on the part of His Excellency, I have received a few letters from different individuals who were interested in the case, some of them in the nature of expressing their appreciation and gratitude as to the course which was taken in the matter, one or two expressing the hope that at some future time it might be possible to extend a further measure of clemency in the case of this particular prisoner. No formal application and no suggestion of further clemency, except of the nature I have described, have been made and the matter is not therefore at the present time under consideration.

I would like to elicit the sympathy of the Prime Minister, of the Minister of Justice, and of the whole cabinet on behalf of Mrs. Robinson, who is imprisoned for a crime which she was forced to commit. There is no doubt that this poor woman had to face a position which no other woman was confronted with since the time of Eve. I am sure that if the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice should consider this matter care-

fully they will come to the conclusion that each hour and each minute this poor woman remains in prison is a blot on the justice of this country. I shall not go into the details of this horrible crime, and when I call it a horrible crime I do not refer to what this unfortunate woman did, but to what she was forced into by her monstrosity of a husband. I hope the Minister of Justice, and the Prime Minister particularly who we all know has a sympathetic heart will have mercy on this unfortunate woman.
Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

["One would naturally expect that when the Minister of Public Works is submitting his estimates to Council, for the consideration of that body, he would supply them with better data than he furnishes this House to justify council in passing the estimates. There does not seem to be any system whereby he can reach a conclusion regarding the absolute need of buildings or the wisdom or otherwise of erecting buildings in these places. He has a request from somebody and cannot tell us. in some cases, from whom Not from the Post Office Department, the Post Office Department does not seem to give him any information whether there is a need for a public building or not. He does not seem to go to the trouble of making any inquiries from the Post Office Department or from any other source as to what the population of the place is or what its needs are. In defending the building of a post office costing about $20,000 in one place he said that it was on a railway. He could find places of three, four, or five times the size and importance of that place on railways all over this country that have no nublic buildings and no post offices erected by the government. I think that is no justification at all and no information.
