House resumed at eight o'clock."]

Mr. Speaker, before that motion is carried I would like to draw the attention of the government to matters of legislation that, I think, should be attended to. Over a week ago this House dealt with two measures to amend the Railway Act, and saw fit at the instance of the government, to send these measures to the Railway Committee for consideration. These Bills passed their second reading in this House, and then at the instance of the government they were sent to the Railway Committee. That is over a week ago and the Railway Committee has not yet met to consider these Bills. When it does meet it will be so congested with Private Bills that these public measures which provide a remedy for evils which the people of Canada are suffering under will be relegated to the background. The government is responsible for sending these Bills to the Railway Committee, and the government should see that they are dealt with there. I, with other members of the House, am opposed to sending these Public Bills to committees appointed to deal with private legislation, but as the gov-' ernment has taken the responsibility of that course they should see that no delay occurs. We all know that these Bills are necessary legislation in the interest of the country, and that if they are not dealt with early in the session and reported to the House, the government will later on have taken all the sittings for government business, and even though the committee should report in favour of them, if they are presented to the House at that stage they would only be so much waste paper. I appeal to the Prime Minister to see that these Bills are dealt with by the Railway Committee immediately.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The committees of the House are under the control of the House itself and not under the control of the government. I believe that had the attention of the chairman of the Railway Committee been directed to this matter he would have promptly called the committee together. I shall deem it my duty to call his attention to it at once.
When does the Minister of Finance intend to introduce the Banking Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not for some little time. There are one or two measures before the House which in due course will, I hope, be referred to committee, and if so I shall ask them -to be detained in the committee until other legislation is brought forward. The matter has engaged our attention, but I fear I will not be able to promise the Bill before the Christmas recess. In the meantime there are other matters concerning my department which will engage our attention.
Is there any probability that the budget speech will be delivered before Christmas?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would like if possible that it should be, but I will make an announcement with reference to it next week.
There is so much delay in bringing down the Naval Bill that we might take some of the legislation of the Finance Department if it were ready.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are a large number of measures to be dealt with.
Mountains of them.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Quebec Province Immigrant buildings generally, $5,000.
PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works.) This is to make provision for repairs to various immigration buildings. $5,000 was voted last year and $975 expended.
How many immigrant buildings are there in Quebec?

There is one at Montreal, one at Nominingue, one at Peri-bonka, one at Roberval and one at Quebec, also others. Each year it has been customary to take a vote for making repairs to the immigrant buildings and to cover what is not otherwise provided for.

I think we shall have to have some further information on this vote. The difficulty about discussing these matters arises from the fact that the minister who is concerned in the public works for which the vote is taken makes it his business to be absent. The ministers who are concerned in the votes ought to make a point of

being here when they are being put through. If they do not, their absence is going to retard the business very much. I would like to know what the policy of the minister is in regard to the construction of immigrant buildings at these small places?

If my hon. friend desires, I will allow this item to stand until the Minister of the Interior can be here.
Item allowed to stand.
Roberval Public Building-revote of $1,000 lapsed, $15,000.

This building is required for post office purposes. There was an appropriation last session of $5,000, out of which we paid $4,000 for a site in April, 1909. The lot has a frontage of 70 feet by a depth of 170 feet. Roberval is a rapidly growing town. It has three churches-two Roman Catholic and one Episcopal, twenty-one stores, three hotels, three flour mills, a branch bank, telegraph and express office. The population of the town is somewhat over 3,000. The revenue is $3,334.18. The money orders issued amount to $30,168.10 and the money orders paid amount to $22,443.79.
Was there arbitration on the site?
I regret that I am unable to tell my hon. friend at this moment, as my deputy is absent, but will be here shortly.
What is the total cost?
It is estimated at $25,000, exclusive of the site.
Will that cover lighting and heating?
Yes.
Is it the custom of the minister to grant to towns of 3,000 inhabitants and with a similar amount of revenue, a public building similar to the one he proposes to build at Roberval?

To a certain extent that is correct. We have laid it down as a principle that a county town, with a population of 2,000 or 3,000, might very well be given a public building; but we have not decided as to when that should be done. We cannot give all the county towns public buildings at once. We have to proceed gradually, according to our financial ability; but speaking generally, I myself would be favourable to giving a county town, with a population of 2,000 or 3,000 people, a public building at as early a date as possible. Of course, if the town has ample post office accommodation, situated in a good building and suited to the requirements of the people, we might very well postpone for a considerable time the erection of a public building.

Does the minister
set apart a certain portion of the moneys of the department for the building of post offices in towns of about 3,000 inhabitants or is it only to party friends that he allots this money?
I may say no to both my hon. friend's questions.

Is there any particular policy about it or is it all surmise? It would be well if the public could have some idea of what may be expected in these matters. For instance, some years ago I brought to the attention of Sir William Mulock, then the Postmaster General, the post office at Grimsby, a post office that produces a revenue of over $4,000, serving a population in the village of 1,400 or 1,500 and including the immediate surrounding portion of the township of North Grimsby which is thickly settled by fruit farmers, a population of about 3,000. The postmaster's salary is about $1,300 and he is allowed a rental of $120 a year for the use of his store where the space for the accommodation of the public is about four feet by perhaps eighteen or twenty-five feet, so that in inclement weather hundreds of people have to wait on the sidewalk for their mails as not more than two or three dozen people can enter the post office at once. Sir William promised that he would have this remedied within a year but nothing has been done yet.
Is this a county town?
No.
Are there any public buildings in the county?

There are in the county, certainly. Grimsby is half way between the two county towns, Hamilton and St. Catharines. It is a very prosperous and up to date place. The people of Grimsby and the district being engaged largely in the fruit business, have a great deal of correspondence in connection with the disposal of their fruit and the postal revenue would justify much better accommodation than they now receive. I am not finding fault with the government for not having erected a public building in that particular place, but I do say that when money is being expended for the erection of post offices the fact that a town is not a county town is not important. The government are not using a good system to ascertain whether the needs of the public require increased postal accommodation. There is no need to have better accommodation than the business warrants, but there is a class of places like Grimsby that I think should have some attention from the Public Works Department. The customs business at Grimsby is large but the citizens have to go to Hamilton or St. Catharines to make payments. A build-

ing costing $4,000 or $5,000 could be built there with the customs office up stairs and the post office down stairs. It would be a mighty good investment for the country. I hope that next year the minister will do something to bring about a more equitable and fair arrangement, generally speaking, throughout the country to serve the people in regard to these public buildings.

I would judge from what my hon. friend says that speaking in a general way the town of Grimsby is about of equal importance, from the standpoint of post office receipts and business, with the town of Roberval, in regard to which we are now asking a vote for a public building. But, if I know anything about the people of Grimsby, I am satisfied that they would not be content to have a public building erected there for post office and customs purposes not to cost more than $4,000. If my hon. friend, speaking on behalf of the people of Grimsby, is prepared to say that they would desire a public building and would be thoroughly satisfies with a building costing $4,000, I would take the matter into my favourable consideration with a view to complying with their request.

I shall take the minister up right now on that, he can take it right into his serious consideration forthwith, because many prominent people in Grimsby have told me that $4,000 would build a building that would give five times as much accommodation as we are now getting, for which the country is paying $120 a year. They said that the interest on a building of $4,000, at the rate at which the government can borrow money, would involve little more expense than the $120 rent which is now paid annually, and for which ipracticajlly no acteommodation !is obtained. The people of Grimsby would be very glad indeed, rather than have the present state of affairs continue, to see a little, narrow $4,000 building built there that would accommodate them. The people of Grimsby know that they cannot expect such a building as a city or large town would have but they do think that the revenue they pay entitles them to a better service and more accommodation than they now enjoy. The people of Grimsby would thank the minister if he would erect a $4,000 building as soon as possible.

The minister has spoken several times of county towns, justifying his expenditure where it was not otherwise justifiable largely upon the fact that although the population was very sparse, still it was a county town. I submit to the hon. minister that that is no justification for expenditure, if the expenditure be not otherwise justifiable, and he ought to revise his opinion. In any case there can be no additional claim by reason of the fact alone 30
that the place is a county town. I do not understand that this government erects the public buildings required for the administration of the law or municipal government. What reason therefore is there why a small place of two or three thousand inhabitants should be supplied with a public building while places with a population of from five to ten thousand are denied the same accommodation, and denied it simply because they do not happen to be county towns? We are continually getting these lame excuses, these palpably unfair excuses, for the expenditure of public money, and I hope, therefore, the hon. minister will change his policy and not select county towns, no matter how small and insignificant, in preference to larger and more important towns.

I would like to call the attention of the hon. minister again to the claims of Parry Sound. That town fulfils all the requirements stated by the minister as essential. It is a county town with a population of four or five thousand. It has a postal revenue of over $9,000 per year, and during the last fiscal year the Postmaster General's report shows that the post office money orders issued there exceeded $200,000. It is also a customs port with a revenue of over $50,000 per year and is quite a large and progressive town, and so far it has not any public building. Last session I drew the matter to the attention of the minister and he said he would consider it and I again call his attention to it.

I have had the claims of Parry Sound under (Consideration. When my hon. friend brought the matter up last session, I said that I was considering the possibility of erecting a public building there; but as my hon. friend knows, there were, very few votes for public buildings in the estimates of last session, and in the estimates now' under consideration there are few new items. They are nearly all for public works provided for two years ago, but which were allowed to stand over. I fully realize the fact that Parry Sound is a growing town, and that it has claims for a public building, and I do not think it will be long before I shall ask parliament to recognize its legitimate claim.

Might I bring to the notice of the minister the claims of the town of Campbellford? It is a flourishing town with a population of probably 3,000 and a postal revenue of between $5,000 and $6,000 and a customs revenue of about $15,000. Our assessed valuation is slightly over a million dollars. There is not a government building in the riding I have the honour to represent, and I think we are entitled to a customs house and post office combined. I know that all



I have to do is to bring, this matter to the notice of the minister and he will grant my request.

I should like to know by what process the minister arrives at his estimates of the population of the different towns he is favouring with public buildings. Roberval. he said, was a place with a population of 3,000 and so on. Well, the official figures show that the population is but 1,248.
My hon. friend is taking the village of Roberval as it was in 1901.

I am taking the last official figures, and these are the figures which are given us in the case of other places in Ontario or Quebec. If we take the estimates given by other parties, we know how utterly unreliable they are, so that we have to fall back on the official figures, except in the case of some town which is growing very fast. I have frequently drawn attention to the fact that the riding I represent has not a single public building. We have not any place in which we can do our customs work, and have to go to Toronto to get anything through the customs in the district where I live. I have been informed by the manager of one of the leading concerns in the town which I represent that they have to put goods through the customs house amounting to a million of dollars annually, and one can easily imagine what trouble ai d difficulty that entails on that firm. Perhaps the postal business is not suffering to the same extent, but it is utterly unfair that the minister should leave these places out and give his preference to places with a revenue of a thousand dollars and sometimes less, simply because larger places do not happen to elect government supporters. After all it is the public money which is spent on these buildings, and when a constituency sends a representative to parliament it does so on other grounds than simply the amount of public money spent there. It is not right that the minister should single out those smaller places for the erection of public works and discriminate against more important places simply because the latter do not favour the government. I hope he will revise his method of determining in what places he will put up public buildings and select instead places yielding the largest postal revenue and which have no public buildings. He is now putting up public buildings in such places as Roberval and other little villages in Quebec and Ontario and the other provinces, which entail an average annual expenditure of $2,400 each, when an expenditure of $300 or $400 at the outside would be ample. In fact, I have heard of Mr. OWEN.
one place, not in my riding, where the people do not want the government to put up a post office. They said that the government would be called upon to pay an enormous amount to some favourite for a site and that would remove the property from the tax roll.
Might I ask the name?

I will give it when I am ready. I said it was not in my riding. I think it is time to look at this thing seriously. It is a serious matter when we are rolling up a vast debt in this country, going to the old country and borrowing money to put up these buildings in places where the country gets no Teturn for years to come. When we are obliged to borrow enormous sums of money annually to meet this deficiency, it is time that we put' an end to the custom of a minister carrying through the estimates of another department when the minister charged with that department is not here to justify the expenditure. Some of us might wish to inquire as to the necessity of this public building, and there^ is no one here to give us any information about it. That is altogether wrong. There is no one here to tell us whether this post office ought to be built or not. Did the hon. gentleman go to the Postmaster General and get him to say that this place was in sad need of a post office, and that there would be a return from the -office that would justify its erection? Nothing of the kind. But somebody comes down from the riding and says: We want so much money spent in this riding; and the hon. gentleman will tell us that he cannot put up a post office in some place where it is much needed because he is building a wharf ot something else there. What in the world has that got to do with it? If a post office is needed, it ought to be put up; and if it is not needed, it ought not to be put up. It seems to me this whole thing is altogether wrong.

Last year the minister put in the estimates a sum of $5,000, if my memory serves me right, for the erection of a post office in the town of Grand-Mere. I do not see such an amount in the estimates for this year. I would like to know why it is that the minister has failed to put in such an amount this year for a post office in a place of the importance of Grand-Mere? Grand-Mere has a population of considerably over 5,000; I could not say what the revenue is, but I am sure there is sufficient revenue to justify the government in allotting the amount which I mentioned. I would ask the hon. gentleman to tell me whether he will make such a provision during the course of the present session.

I may say to my hon. friend that it is quite true that two years

ago there was an amount put in the estimates for a public building at Grand-Mere, and I have left it out of the estimates this year. But I may say to him that my attention had not been called to the urgent necessity of that building at Grand-Mere, and as I had not heard from my hon. friend on the subject, I thought perhaps the matter was not extremely urgent, and that possibly there might be sufficient post office accommodation at present, and that the erection of a new building might be postponed, at all events, for a short time. Therefore, there is no item in the estimates for this building, and I am not able to give my hon. friend any assurance as to when a public building will be undertaken there. Now, with regard to Campbellford, which has been so forcibly presented to my attention by my hon. friend from East Northumberland (Mr. Owen), and who also mentioned the necessity for a public building during the last session of parliament. I will say to him now, as I said then, that I am impressed With the arguments he has advanced, and I think the claims of Campbellford are entitled to my careful consideration. A little later I will have the matter more carefully looked into, and I trust it will be possible before long to take the necessary steps towards the erection of a public building at Campbellford.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright), I desire to say that he does me a great injustice when he makes the statement to this committee that we pick out places for the erection of public works simply in view of the support which we have got from the constituencies. If it were necessary, I could appeal to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, going over different constituencies all the way from Prince Edward Island to the Pacific ocean, and I am sure that if the hon. members from these constituencies were to rise in their places, they would bear testimony to the fact that I have endeavoured to do complete justice to the various constituencies which they represent, as well as to those which have returned supporters of the government. Let me ask the hon. member who represents the district of Nipissing (Mr. Gordon) whether he thinks the charge of the hon. member for Muskoka is well founded. Let me ask the hon. member who represents the constituency of Digby (Mr. Jameson) if he thinks the charge is well founded. Let me ask my hon. friend who represents the constituency of Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) if he thinks the charge is well founded. Let me ask my hon. friend who represents the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) if he thinks the charge is well founded. The people of St. John, by a majority of the votes, supported the hon. gentleman who represents that city, and whom I do not now 30i
see in his place. I might go all over the Dominion of Canada, I might go to the city of Vancouver, to the city of Victoria, to the city of New Westminster and to various other constituencies in the province of British Columbia, and the hon. gentleman will find that I have recognized the legitimate claims of the various sections of th^t province, entirely irrespective of political and party considerations. Go to the city of Toronto, a city which for years has been sending only members in opposition to this government, and where we are spending, not merely $100,000, but in the vicinity of $700,000 in much needed improvements. I say we might go all over the Dominion, and the facts will show that I have endeavoured, and it has been my honest endeavour, so far as I possibly could, to recognize the legitimate claims of the various sections of Canada. I know there are many public buildings and there are many wharfs which ought to be attended to, but we are not able to do all these things at once'. I am doing all I can with the limited amount of money which has been placed at my disposal by the Minister of Finance, and' have endeavoured to meet the most urgent needs, and have done so, as I say, entirely irrespective of political and party considerations. It is a matter of regret to me that I am not able now to meet the demands of all sections of the country, but the best I can do is to attend to those needs as I have the means of doing. So I can assure my hon. friends opposite that any legitimate demands which they present to me for consideration with respect to public buildings, wharfs, dredging, or other improvements, will receive my most careful consideration, Now one word with regard to the erection of public buildings in the smaller towns. Some hon. gentlemen opposite take the view that any kind of a building is good enough for the smaller towns and cities throughout the country, and that we ought not to put up a public building in any city or town where the interest upon the cost and the expense ol caretaking will amount to more than the postal revenue. Now, Sir, I entirely disagree with that proposition. In the larger cities, in the city of Ottawa, in the city of Montreal, in the city of Toronto and other larger cities of Canada, when we are proceeding to erect public buildings, we do not limit the class of building to one which is immediately sufficient _ for the purpose, but we look to the question of beauty, we look to the providing in that city of a public building of which the people will be proud, in which they will take a just pride and which they can point to strangers as being worthy of the Dominion of Canada. Now, if that is the case, why should we not do a little something in the smaller cities and towns towards the erection of suitable public buildings which will be somewhat ornamen-

tal in character and to which the people in those communities can point with pride and say, this is a public building which has been given us by the Dominion of Canada. In the great majority of these towns there is no other public expenditure. They have no harbours to be dredged, they have no navigable channels to be improved, there are no wharfs to be built, and the only public expenditure which they get is the small amount of money which may be expended in the erection of a public building. Therefore, I am prepared to say that so long as I remain Minister of Public Works I shall give reasonable and fair consideration to the' requests which may be made to me for the construction of public buildings in the thriving towns throughout Canada no matter in which counties they may be situate and no matter what may be the political complexion of the representatives whom they send to parliament.

I am delighted to hear the remarks made by the Minister of Public Works. I am not inclined to too severely criticise him, but as he has made the statement that his aim as Minister of Public Works is to distribute public money over this country regardless of what maybe the political complexion of any particular constituency, I have a case right in point. He did not ask me, he asked others, but I think I might as well state the situation with reference to my own constituency. There is the constituency of Brandon and there is the constituency of Souris immediately south of Brandon. Brandon has had hundreds of thousands of dollars of expenditure in it because it was the home of the late Minister of the Interior, while the constituency which I have the honour to represent, lying immediately south of Brandon, has never had one dollar of public money expended in it although I have several times, during the last two or three years, tried to bring the claim of my town and my constituency before the Minister of Public Works. I do not ask for a large amount of money. I do not just exactly agree with the Minister of Public Works that it is necessary to expend as large an amount of money in a town of 2,000 or 3,000 inhabitants for a post office as it would be in a larger place. If you could erect a solid brick building, say, 30 x 50 or 60 feet in dimensions for $6,000 or $8,000 I know you would have a very good building, and I believe it would be adequate for post office purposes in any of these towns and that these towns would be very glad to get it; in fact, if a larger amount were expended upon such a building they would consider it a matter of extravagance. The town of Souris is in the constituency of the late Minister of the Interior and the late Minister of the Interior has the town of Souris to thank for his seat at the present time. He formerly had a Mr. PUGSLEY.
majority of some 800 or 900 but he came out of the last election with a majority of 65. I brought up the question of the dismissal of the postmaster at Souris, another which must be added to disgraceful acts of the late Minister of the Interior in connection with that post office. He turned a man out of that office who had held it for years and years and who had gone to considerable expense in preparing the office according to the instructions of the inspector. But, that is not what I am talking about now. The town of Souris and my own town of Boisse-vain are about the same size. I have asked the Minister of Public Works to give me a post office in Boissevain. I think that for $12,000 you can buy a corner site _ in the centre of the town and erect the building. I believe a site can be secured for between $3,500 and $4,000 and the remainder will erect a building with which we will be well satisfied. I find that the little town of Souris is down in the estimates this year for $15,000 for a public building. I have been unable to get anything. Will any hon. member of this House say that the political complexion of the constituency of Brandon had nothing to do with putting $15,000 into Souris and nothing to do with absolutely refusing to give me anything for my constituency. I think the minister will have to take back some of the arguments he used in that respect. I could not present to this House a better argument to show that the political complexion of the constituencies is very largely taken into _ account in giving necessary public buildings to this country. However, he has got so near to my constituency now that _ I want to put in a plea for the town of Boissevain to be considered and I want to express the hope that in the supplementarv estimates provision will be made for a $12,000 building in that town.
What is the population of Boissevain?
About 1,300.
Will my hon. friend guarantee me against the most-I shall not say violent-but against attack from the other side?
Yes, sir, I will defend you against all comers.

I would like to know if the minister justifies this Roberval vote on the ground that it is the county town aside from the question of whether the business requirements of the place warrant the expenditure?

No, I did not mention that Roberval was the county town, but I understand that Roberval has a population of some 3,000 and that it is a rapidly growing town. Its population has increased

from 1,248 in 1901 to something over 3,000 at the present time.
Where does the minister get his figures as to population?
I am told that it is a county town as well.
The hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) referred to the census figures as, I think, 1,200. Where would the minister get any figures showing the population since that time?

We had a petition from the municipal council of the town, but I do not know whether that states the population or not. Then, we have an assurance from the member for the county that the population is over 3,000. I made inquiry from other sources and that is verified.

Certainly the minister made some reference to the rule upon which the department has been acting as to the propriety of public buildings being erected in county towns, but I think he laid it down that there must also exist the condition that there is no other public building in the riding.

I did not lay down any hard and fast rule. What I said was that it had been laid down as a rule that each county in the Dominion might fairly claim a public building and that, as a rule, that could be placed in the county town, but I did not say that there should never be more than one building in a county. There might be a county town, a thriving town, and there might be another town somewhat larger and at a considerable distance away from the county town. One cannot lay down a hard and fast rule.

I understood the minister to lay down the rule that the Minister of Finance laid down two or three years ago and that was that claims would be recognized for public buildings in county towns and in constituencies in which there was no other public building. That is the rule, as I understood the Minister of Finance to lay it down a few years ago, and the one which I understand the Minister of Public Works to rely upon this afternoon.
In what constituency is Roberval?
Chicoutimi and Saguenay.
Are there no other public buildings in that county?
There is one at Chicoutimi.

Roberval is the chief town of the county of Lake St. John. Lake St. John and Saguenay, for local purposes,
are two distinct counties, and they are of immense territory, occupying the northern part of the province of Quebec and extending as far as Labrador. In that federal district there are two chief towns for judicial purposes, and Roberval has a population of at least 3,000.
Was there any request from the Post Office Department for this building?
I assume there was not or otherwise I would have a record of it here.
On whose request was the building erected?
There was a petition presented from the municipal council of the town of Roberval, and also a strong recommendation from Mr. Girard, the member for the constituency.
Is it not a rule that the Post Office Department should send a requisition to the Public Works Department for a building which it considers necessary?
It is not the rule.
Is it not customary?
It is not.
Was there an arbitration on the value of this site which cost $4,000?
No. We sent Mr. Gin-gras, clerk of works at Montreal, who reported this was a fair and reasonable price.
Did the owner offer it for $4,000 in the first instance?
He wanted more, and Mr. Gingras recommended $4,000 as a fair price. The lot is a large one having a frontage of 70 feet and a depth of 170.
I understood the minister to tell us the other night that it was the practice of the department to have the [DOT] value of these sites determined by arbitration.

I did not intend to convey that it was a general practice. We did it in the case of the St. Roch property, and the arbitrators in that case were: Thomas M. McCarthy, O.E., acting for the government, J. A. Gignac for the property owners and Joseph Gauthier was the third arbitrator. We have in the department some officers who are accustomed to value property and upon whose judgment we rely when we do not have arbitration.
Upon whose recommendation -was the government arbitrator in the St. Roch case appointed?
My recollection is that in that -case I consulted with the Prime Minister. We satisfied ourselves that he was a reliable man and acquainted with the value of property.

The minister spoke about buildings that the people could point to with pride as beautiful in architecture and meritorious from the aesthetic point of view, and that is all very well if we had money to burn. But the minister is limited in his expenditure on these buildings, and the business people of the country would prefer to have ten $10,000 buildings suitable to accommodate the business offering rather than five $20,000 buildings which wrere not necessary except as beautiful pictures.
Would the hon. gentleman say that, in reference to these build, ings in Ottawa which could be erected for half the money if they were plain buildings?	[DOT]
This is the capital of the Dominion and the buildings here are a concern of national pride, and you cannot compare them with a post office building in a small town of 3,000 inhabitants.
But why waste money on ornamentation?

The buildings in the capital city of this Dominion are in a different position altogether from the small buildings in country towns, and even in the capital it is just a question whether you should not erect buildings free from expensive ornamentation but which would supply twice as much space and light in which to transact the business of the country.
Does the hon. gentleman think that in a town where the people take a pride in their private buildings, we should put up a plain building -which the citizens would be ashamed of?
That is the other extreme, and I do not go that far.
What we should aim at is to be moderate in our expenditure.
Yes.

And at the same time recognize that these people in the smaller towns are just as much a part of the Dominion as are the people in the larger cities. My hon. friend from the constituency in which the town of Boissevain is situated stated that the town of Souris gave to the Hon. Mr. Sifton a majority, and so saved his election in that constituency, and that is the reason why we are giving it a public building. My information is that the town of Souris went strongly Conservative in the Mr. CROCKET.
last election, giving a majority against Mr. Sifton. So that the reason assigned by my hon. friend falls to the ground.
If the minister looks up the figures, he will find that although Souris is strongly Conservative, the majority was very small.
It seems to me that the item for that building first appeared in the estimates before the general election, when it gave a different majority.
Yes, it appeared before the general election.

The hon. gentleman referred to Nipissing as one of the constituencies which has been fairly treated in the matter of public buildings. I am pleased to be able to say that that is tthe case. In fact, the minister has done more than I expected. I want to speak fairly and frankly. In North Bay, which is a county town, and which yields a postal revenue of $12,000 or $14,000, a good building has been erected. For Sudbury I notice an appropriation of $20,000 in the estimates this year. That town produces a postal revenue of $8,000 or $10,000, and is larger than any of the towns mentioned here to-day. The town of Cobalt, which has a population of over 6,000, while there are over 12,000 people in the immediate vicinity, has at present very poor postal accommodation. I called the minister's attention to -this last session, and he told me that owing to the falling revenues of the country he could no-t do anything then; but I hope that this year he can see his way clear to do something. The fact of the minister being pretty fair to Nipissing I attribute to our asking for public buildings only in places which absolutely require them. I thank the minister very much for what he has done for us, and I hope he will keep on in the good work.

I am delighted to hear that my hon. friend from Nipissing is so well satisfied with what the Minister of Public .Works has done for his riding. I would be delighted if I could say the same thing about my riding, but things are entirely different there. In almost every part of the riding where I went las-t fall, I found that public works of various kinds had been promised from the platform; but in looking over the estimates I find that only two points in my riding have been taken notice of at all-Providence Bay and Little Current. The town of Sudbury, which my hon. friend from Nipissing has mentioned, is a growing town which, in the near future, will be a city. The Ontario government has spent a great deal of money in erecting public buildings there. My hon. friend is satisfied with an appropriation of $20,000 for

a public building in Sudbury, whereas a little town of 1,500 inhabitants is getting a $25,000 post office.
$20,000 is only the start.
Perhaps the minister will give us the estimated cost of the post office at Sudbury?
I will get the information when we come .to that item; but the amount of $20,000 is only for the work to be done during the coming , year.

I will be delighted if the the minister will take notice that there are some very large towns giving large revenues to the Post Office Department in my constituency which have great need of good buildings; for instance, the town of Thessa-lon with a population of 2,000, Blind River with a population of over 3,000, Massey, Webbwood, Gore Bay, Little Current and Manitowaning; and they would be entirely satisfied with buildings costing $4,000 or $5,000. So, while everybody is asking the minister to think of their Tidings, I hope, out of the goodness of his heart, he will not forget the most important Tiding in the province of Ontario.
Are Sault Ste. MaTie and Michipicoten in the hon. gentleman's riding?
No.

I am not going to ask the minister out of the goodness of his heart to do anything for me. I take for granted that this country can afford to pay officials to attend to the public business. I take for granted that there is a Post Office Department that knows its needs and is able to communicate them to another department. If that were done in a businesslike way, I would not be placed in the humiliating position of having from time to time to come here and urge the necessity of a post office at Lethbridge. The difficulty is that the minister seems to think that his function is to please certain people, whereas it seems to me that the function of parliament is to spend the public money where the requirements of the people demand it. I put a question to the hon. member a few days ago. I asked him in simple English :
Has the Post Office Department made any demand or representation to the Public Works Department for better post office accommodation in the city of Lethbridge?
Evidently the hon. gentleman thought himself exceedingly clever in the way he answered the question. He did not give me the information I asked, if he had I would have been satisfied. He told me a story about the building that was erected in
Lethbridge in 1892 or 1893, which he said was used for customs and inland revenue purposes.

May I say to my hon. friend that when I received the answer from my department I (thought myself there possibly might have been some later request to which my hon. friend was referring, but I am informed by my deputy and was then informed that there had been no late request from the Postmaster General and therefore the answer was correct.

I should be very sorry to misrepresent the hon. gentleman or any one else. I do not want to waste the time of the House in matters of this kind but I wish to place before the House the exact situation that exists. The hon. minister does not seem to know it. If he will come to the House when asking for a post office and say that the application is endorsed by the Post Office Department, well and good, but when he says these applications were endorsed by boards of trade and by town councils, it is time for us to have something to say in this matter. I picked up a copy of the Montreal ' Star ' only on Saturday last in which reference was made to the business activities in various cities in this country. It gives a list of 21 cities and refers to the value of the building permits for the month of October. Here is the order in which they stand: Toronto 1; Montreal 2; Winnipeg 3; Vancouver 4; Calgary 5; Hamilton 6, Lethbridge 7; Victoria 8; Fort William 9; Edmonton 10. Thus Lethbridge stands next to Hamilton.
Is that not simply the percentage of increase?

It is the actual building permits for October, 1909. The city of Lethbridge last year had a postal revenue of $19,000 and I venture to say that by now it has reached $25,000 a year, and they are suffering from the lack of postal facilities. I do not want the money of this country shoved into Lethbridge to put up buildings, the people going in there can put up the buildings, but I want to see the people there put in a position to attend to their business in a proper way and if it is a question of getting petitions. from boards of trade or city councils, the hon. gentleman can get all he wants. Political snipes went through that constituency at the time I was running that election, saying: It is no use electing this man; you want a post office and if you elect him you will not get it. Yet, in the face of that, the hon. gentleman gets up here and says there is no politics in this matter. Is the hon. gentleman satisfied from the clipping I have sent him that the reference was to building permits?
Yes, the hon. gentleman seems to be correct.

Lethbridge stands next to Hamilton and Edmonton, which stands 10th on the list, has a $200,000 building while Lethbridge has nothing. The hon. gentleman knows nothing about the situation there or he would have brought down some appropriation for Lethbridge. This appears to me to be the only opportunity of bringing this matter forward. It is humiliating to have to do this; I do not conceive that the people of Canada sent me here to do this work, I think there is something else to attend to, and if the hon. gentleman had a force of competent men going through the country to pass on these things there would be less said about them in the House. I hope I shall not have to discuss this again and that I have said enough to convince the hon. gentleman of the necessity of granting this building. Every one is crying out for it, and why the minister is giving a small place with a population of 1,300 and a postal revenue of $1,500, a public building costing $25,000, without a request as the hon. gentleman himself admitted, from the Post Office Department or from the Customs Department, is something that I cannot understand in any country where they are attempting to have their affairs administered with some system of business.

What are the rental and salary at present?
_ Mr. PUGSLEY. The postmaster's salary is $1,192 besides $75 for commissions on money orders and $7.65 on postal notes. The rental paid is $175, a total of $1,308.97.
I want to hear from the hon. gentleman about this matter. Has he got this thing thoroughly in the back of his head?

My hon. friend is so genial and he has such a good cause to plead, that I cannot refrain from saying a word in reply. The hon. gentleman sent me a statement of figures showing the number of building permits in Lethbridge, and they show, what I was told when I "was in the west, that Lethbridge has recently taken on a very rapid growth. If my hon. friend will look at these figures which he has sent me he will see that in October, 1908, there was not a single building permit in Lethbridge.
There were building permits but this paper did not get them, that is all.

That may be. At all events, by the statement the hon. gentleman sent me, there does not seem to have been a building permit in Lethbridge in October, 1908. That, of course, would show that there has been a very sudden increase in growth. But I know and my

hon. friend knows that it is within the last year or so that Lethbridge has suddenly begun to forge ahead, and it is forging ahead with great rapidity. I told my hon. friend the other day and I tell him now that I recognize the strong claims of Lethbridge for better postal accommodation. I have unfortunately no amount in these estimates for the purpose, but, as I explained to the committee before, there are very few new items in these estimates, they are mostly for public works provided for two years ago. But I would say to my hon. friend that I will consider carefully the claims of Lethbridge, and if there should be supplementary estimates-I do not know whether there will be-these claims will be noted for consideration in connection with these estimates. I' can make no promise further than may be implied in this statement at the present time, but I beg to assure my hon. friend that no one can recognize more strongly than I do the necessity for giving better postal accommodation in Lethbridge than they have there now.
Will the hon. gentleman take this up with the Post Office Department? He said that there is nothing from the Post Office Department in connection with this matter.
Nothing beyond what was returned to the House.

My information is different, I am sorry to say. I would like to get the minister in touch with the Post Office Department. I am sorry to have to say that if the Post Office Department does not know its business better than that there is something wrong there. I was given to understand the hon. gentleman had been written to about this matter in April last by the Post Office Department.
I understood the minister to say that there was some requisition from the sitting member for the county. Will he read that communication?
I have not the communication here but can give the gist of it.
We ought to have the document itself.

I cannot give it now. The effect of the communication was that the town was increasing rapidly, that it has a population of over 3,000, that numerous tourists frequent it in the summer months, that the post office is in the postmaster's house and not at all suited to the public convenience, and that, in the interest of the good reputation of the Dominion, a public building should be provided adequate to the wants of this growing town.

That is a very nice statement, but it would be only fair to the committee that the minister should bring' down the letter itself. It would be interesting to have that part of the communication which he has not quoted, and I suppose he has no objection to bringing down the letter.
None whatever, but I have really stated all it contains.
What we are trying to find out is, if possible, the policy of the department in the construction of public buildings.
That policy is to construct, to as reasonable an extent as possible, public buildings where they are required in the public interests.

Of course we could not expect the hon. minister to say anything else, but I think he was rather severe in his criticism of my hon. friend from Muskoka. My hon. friend suggested that possibly somewhere in the department there was political partisanship, and if that suspicion be aroused, the government is responsible for it. Before the hon. gentleman was Minister of Public Works the department had a clear cut policy, well understood in the country. Prior to the general election of 1900, the Department of Public Works sent out a letter, a copy of which I have under my hand. The late Mr. Tarte, who was then Minister of Public Works, had absented himself a little while from the department, and Sir William Mullock, who was then Postmaster General, was acting in his stead, and Sir William Mullock sent out a circular to Reform members of parliament and defeated government candidates, but was careful to leave out altogether Conservative members and the defeated Conservative candidates. In that circular he called upon those to whom it was sent to state what public buildings they wanted in their counties, whether they would recommend that the contracts be given after public competition, and also a number of other inquiries along that line.
Perhaps he was merely seeking information.

But it was rather peculiar that he only sought it from government supporters. My hon. friend says there is no partisanship in his department. Would he then explain how this circular came to be sent to government members and government defeated candidates and not to any others?
Sir William Mulock may not have thought that hon. gentleman opposite would give him the information he required.

There is another reason far more likely. My hon. friend ought certainly to be sparing in his criticisms on my hon. friend from Muskoka, who suggested that somewhere in the department there was a taint of political partisanship. Who can be responsible for that suspicion, if not the government that sent out a circular of that kind, more especially as the circular was issued shortly before the general election of 1900 and read on the public platform in every province. The hon. minister cannot therefore complain if the public suspect that instead of spending public money where the public interests may best be served, he selects here and there a county, where the issue is uncertain, and where it would be likely such expenditure would have the greatest effect, and where the proposed expenditure for the purposes of erecting a public building or a wharf or _ doing some dredging in that locality might influence the public vote in the government's behalf. Since the hon. gentleman will not explain what the policy of his department is now, we are perfectly justified in assuming that this policv, which was inaugurated in 1900, is still in force. I understand my hon. friend to say he will bring down the letter.
I will.
Perhaps in the future it will be better for the hon. gentleman to produce the original documents than give synopses of them.
Not unless specially desired.
It would be less troublesome for the department to give him the letter itself, than to copy passages out of it which might suit his purpose.

These selections which I have quoted never came to my knowledge, but were simply made by the officials of the department with the view of giving the requisite information as to who had applied for public works. I had no more to do with the selections than my hon. friend.
Rock Island public building, $5,000.

This is to provide for the purchase of a site and the erection of a public building in the village of Rock Island, Stanstead county. The proposed building is required for post office and customs purposes. I may say that this matter had been under consideration some little time, and when first pressed upon my attention by the member for that constituency, I made particular inquiries of the Minister of Customs. He in turn inquired of the officials of his department and I am in a position to say that this building is urgently required there for customs purposes, and I can say the same with regard to its necessity for post office purposes.

Rock Island is close to the boundary between Canada and the United States, and it is necessary to give accommodation there for the customs officials. A good deal of postal business also is done there.
What is the population?
It was only 615 in 1901, but has grown considerable since.
What is the revenue?
$3,013-very much larger than one would expect from its comparatively small population.
What is to be the cost of the building?
From $15,000 to $20,000 including the site.
What is the cost of the service?
Salary $1,252, besides commissions on money orders. The rent is $175 per annum.
Will the hon. minister read the requisition from the Customs Department?
The commissioner came to the department and gave verbal assurance that this building was urgently needed. This item was agreed to after consideration extending over several weeks.
How many customs officers are there permanently?
I cannot say, but quite a number. Then some three miles away from Rock Island there is another place where a good deal of customs business is transacted. But Rock Island is the principal place.
Has there been any d.emand for this particular service from the Post Office Department?
No demand from the Post Office Department.

I think the time has arrived in this country when these departments that are being served should be hel l responsible. I realize that the hon. gentleman is in a very disagreeable position, he has to put these matters through. I say that these departments which are being served should be held responsible, and the hon. gentleman should not be allowed to pass an item until he produces evidence from the department that they need the service.
I would like to know whether Rock Island is a customs port.
I think the actual customs port is about three miles away, at Beebe Plain, but Rock Island is an important place.
How far is Rock Island from Stanstead Plain?

Rock Island itself is not the customs port, but it is the place at which the customs work of the port of Stanstead is done. Stanstead village which, in years gone by, used to be an important village, has not grown, while Rock Island is a manufacturing and industrial place on the border line, and has been growing rapidly. I think it has a population of about 3,000.
The Minister of Public Works told us it was 615.
I gave that population as of nine years ago.
I have been there several times, and I was told the population was about 3,000.
My information is that there are twelve stores, two hotels, a grist mill and ten factories at Rock Island; also a bank, and the ordinary express and telegraph offices.
Is it intended to close down the customs office at the other town?

The real business of the Customs Department is now being done at a place called Stanstead Junction, which is, I think, a little over two miles to the west of Rock Island. The reason the business is done there is that it is a junction of the railway. But Rock Island itself is the place where nearly all the duties are paid, being an industrial centre. Beebe Plain, where the railway junction is, and where the manifesting is done, is a hamlet of only three or four houses and a railroad station. Rock Island is an important industrial village on the border line; there is a little spur from the railroad which runs up to Rock Island, and which serves the Canadian village as well as the American village. The station is almost on the boundary line. The real business of the port is largely done at Rock Island, and it is at Rock Island that the customs officers want their accommodation.
How many customs officers?

At the whole port, I think five. A part of the work is done at Beebe Plain where the station is.
Shawenegan Falls, revote, $8,000.

This is to make provision for the construction of a public building at Shawenegan Falls. The commit-

tee are aware that Shawenegan Palls is an important manufacturing centre. It has a superior water-power, a large number of factories, and the population is growing rapidly. The population is estimated at 2,300. The postal revenue last year was $2,586, and from the Customs Department, $42,000. The cost of the building will run from $30,000 to $35,000, and is intended to give accommodation, not only to the Post Office Department, but to the Customs and Inland Revenue also. That price does not include the site, which has been given free by the municipality. At present we pay a rental of $175 per annum for the post office, and $143 for customs. The salary of the postmaster, including commissions, is $1,300. That is outside of customs.
Does the hon. gentleman really think a building of that price is required under those circumstances?

I think so. My hon. friend will observe that it is to accommodate three departments, post office, customs and inland revenue. Last year, as I say, the customs revenue amounted to $42,521.53; the year before it was over $80,000, when, I suppose, a considerable quantity of machinery was imported.

There are a great many, places where comparatively small buildings would answer the purpose, costing $10,000 to $12,000, and I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that instead of spending so large a sum of money at a place like Shawenegan Falls, he should spread it over a larger number of places, putting up less expensive buildings. At present he is erecting expensive buildings at some places, and leaving other places, perhaps with a larger population and more business, entirely unserved, or served inadequately.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) has not chosen a good instance to illustrate his theory in the case of Shawenegan Falls. If he does not know, let me tell him that Shawenegan Falls was practically a desert ten years a^o, whereas during the last two years alone between $10,000,000 and $12,000,000 have been invested to develop the water-power. There has been invested by the Northern Aluminum Company, which is a branch of the Pittsburgh Reduction Works, over $2,000,000 in establishing and enlarging their works. Besides, there is a vast amount of capital invested by foreigners, for instance by the Belgo-Canadian Pulp and Paper Company, who are supposed to have the most modern and best equipped pulp and paper mill in Canada. It is true that last year the revenue fell off from the preceding year. In 1907-8 the customs revenue at Shawenegan Falls was $83,539.41, Whilst in 1908-9 it was
$42,521.53. I see that the customs entries have decreased all over the county in the last fiscal year. The population decreased at Shawenegan Falls because of the fact that the Northern Aluminum Company had to close down their works for a while for want of orders. When the aluminum business was started at Shawenegan Falls there was a great demand for the products of this industry and prices were very high. The large prices that they were getting for that commodity caused new mills to spring up and induced those that were already in existence to enlarge their plants. Therefore, there was an over production which caused a falling off in the orders of the Northern Aluminum Company. They had to close down their works for a while which caused a considerable emigration from Shawenegan Falls because a number of men were left without employment. I may say that they have entered into a number of contracts lately and that the shops have been re-opened. They have had a contract from the government of Ontario for a transmission wire for the Hydro-Electric Power Commission. For the last seven months the customs revenue collected at Shawenegan Falls, including the entries for Grand Mere, amounted to $27,367.36.
Would the hon. gentleman tell us the nature of the imports there?

New machinery was imported from the United States to be installed in the Northern Aluminum plant. Machinery is now being imported for a large cotton mill which is being constructed on the same improved principle as the mill of the Wabasso Cotton Company at Three Rivers. They propose to manufacture a finer kind of cotton than is now manufactured by the other mills in Canada. They will manufacture the kind used in underclothing and shirts-what we commonly call linen.
Linen faced?

I do not know what they call it, but it is the linen used in shirts, collars, cuffs, &c. When the Shawenegan Falls was divided into town lots the Shawenegan Water and Power Company, who owned most of the land, would not sell a lot unless the buyer agreed to put un a house of certain dimensions, a certain height and plan and costing so much money. They wanted to have a fine .town.
Does the hon. gentleman remember the minimum amount that they had to spend on each building?

It depended on the street where the building was located. They had to spend more on business streets than on residential streets. I do not know but that certain streets were exempt from that. Shawenegan Falls is a growing town, and

it will grow more in the future because they are putting up new plants every day.

The hon. gentleman has not disposed of the suggestion that I was making to the minister. I am not objecting to Shawenegan Falls or any other part of the country being properly served with a public building, but I do not think that the hon. gentleman has proved that a $10,000 or $12,000 building would not serve that town. You can put up quite a chunk of a building if you are not going in for a lot of style and waste space for $10,000 or $12,000.

Surely my hon. friend does not pretend seriously to assert that you can erect a suitable building for the post office officials, for the accommodation of the public, for the customs officials and for the accommodation of the public doing business with that department, for the inland revenue officials and for the accommodation of the public doing business with that department, provide accommodation for the caretaker, as there must be a caretaker for these public buildings, all that for $10,000-a good substantial building of stone and brick with proper sanitary arrangements, heat and light.
I do.

I have nad a great deal of experience in building and I am unable to agree with my hon. friend. I do not think that a suitable building for the accommodation bf these three departments, such a building as one ought to put up in an important town like Shawenegan, which is destined to be a very important place in the near future, could be erected for less than $30,000.

All you would need in that place is practically three good large rooms. You could erect a building of three, or perhaps two stories, and have three good large rooms in it, one for the post office, another for the customs and another for the Inland Revenue Department, and you could do it for $10,000 or $12,000 if you did not want to waste the money.

I agree with what the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau) has said. I think that if there are any young towns which justify the government in spending money certainly Shawenegan is one of them. I must say that Shawenegan and Grand-Mere have grown and are growing very quickly. I think that before long these towns will have a population of at least 20,000 and it may go beyond tnat mark in the near future. But I must remark that what the hon. gentleman said with reference to Shawenegan Falls applies with doubled force to the town of Grand-Mere. While Mr. BUREAU.
Shawenegan Falls has a population of 2,000 and a few hundred, and while I agree that it has a right to have this public building, we have in Grand-Mere a population of 5,300. While they have a gross total revenue of $2,500 from the post office we have a total revenue of $4,221. I see that the government are spending large sums of money in towns which give little or no promise of future development. For instance, there is the town of Nicolet, which has a gross total revenue of $3,800, and I think I am safe in saying that the post office which the government are building there will not cost less than $20,000 or $30,000. The same applies to Roberval, where the revenue is only $3,300. I would say to the minister that petition after petition has been sent to the government asking for the erection of a public building in Grand-Mere. I remember coming as a delegate to ask the government to erect a post office in that growing town. We were promised that something would be done, but while $5,000 was granted for the erection of a building the government made it a condition that the corporation should supply the land. We did not accept this offer, because we maintained that $5,000 would not erect the building which we would like to see in our town.
That was only to make a start.

I think I have a right to ask the minister to grant us at least $5,000 for a building in Grand-Mere.
St. Henri Post Office-improvements-revote of $270 lapsed, $7,000.

This is to be applied to the erection of a one-story addition to the post office at St. Henri, as requested by the Post Office Department as long ago as 1908. The acting Deputy Postmaster General asked for this extension, and as one argument in favour of it he said that the letter-carriers for St. Cunegonde, Cote St. Paul and St. Henri are massed at the St. Henri depot and that an enlargement of the building is absolutely necessary. The appropriation for 1908-9 was $1,200, of which we expended $930 upon inside improvements and $270 lapsed. The chief architect estimates it would take $7,000 to make the addition required. St. Henri is an important suburb of Montreal.
Will that complete the work?

Yes.
St. Jacques de FAchigan public building, $15,000.

This is to make provision towards the erection of a building for post office purposes. There is a largely

signed petition of the people and also of the' municipal council. The site was purchased in October, 1909, for $3,000; it is 53 feet on the main street by 123. The population at the last census was 2,580.
What is the revenue?
What is to he the cost of the building?

It will not exceed $20,-
000.
Including the site?

Including the site.
Mr. FOSTER, What is the present cost of that post office, salary and rental?
$340, and commissions $42.
Is it in the county of Montcalm?
Yes.
What is the present rental for the building?
Very small, only $38.
Has the minister received any request from the Post Office Department for this building?
No.

The whole revenue here is $779, and with a population of 2,500 in the town, that is not much of an argument for the expenditure of $20,000 on a post office building. We must protest most strongly against this. I agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath) that in these cases there should be a request from the responsible minister of the department whose business is to be conducted in these buildings. I had always supposed that to be done and that there was consultation between the minister for *whose department the building was to be erected and the Minister of Public Works as to what kind of accommodation would be necessary. The moment this building is erected it will mean an annual charge of $2,000 which will swallow up more than three times the entire revenue. I do not know whether this is a growing town or not.
It has a tobacco factory, a branch bank, three saw-mills, and it is on the line of the new Canadian Northern.

Well, it is a large recommendation that it is on a railway line. Is it the policy of the government now to build $25,000 buildings in each county town and $20,000 buildings in each town that is on the line of a railway? This is one of
the worst cases yet, and as a protest against that kind of thing, I move that the vote be reduced by $10,000.
Amendment (Mr. Foster) negatived.
Yeas 17; nays 33.

The practice indulged in by the Minister of Public Works this session is to present an item on behalf of say the Post Office Department, for the erection of a building and then to tell us that he knows nothing about it. In this case he has told us that the request for the building did not originate with the Post Office Department. The Post Office Department is supposed to know the needs of the country for increased postal facilities. The Postmaster General should know how much money is to be expended and having looked over the whole Dominion he would, if his department were properly conducted, select the most deserving cases for public expenditure in view of the means at his disposal. But nothing of this kind is done, and the Minister of Public Works, simply because he gets a petition from some people in a locality,'decides to erect a post office without consulting the Postmaster General as to the necessity for it. The head of the Post Office Department, having determined upon a scheme of public expenditure within the resources of the country, shall submit to the cabinet his proposals, showing just what is required and why it is required. This, having been properly brought before council, it will be or will not be, according as it is considered right, brought in as an estimate and submitted to this committee. If we, a# a committee, do not insist upon procedure of that kind, we are not discharging our duties to our constituents. All these preliminaries have been disregarded in this case. But assuming that they had all been complied with, that is not enough. When the Minister of Public Works submits an estimate to the committee, it is most unreasonable that he should be alone in the matter. He does not profess to have, and we could not expect him to have, a competent knowledge of the requirements. It is absolutely necessary, in the consideration of estimates for another department, that the responsible head of that department should be here to explain why the money is demanded. We are proceeding to-day on an entirely improper basis. We have the fact that no demand has been made by the Post Office Department for this expenditure. We have the fact that the Minister of Public Works has no competent knowledge of the matter. We have the fact that there is no pretense that the Post Office Department has taken a broad, general survey of what should be the expenditure in Canada as a whole, and how that expenditure should be distributed. We are pro-

ceeding on a piece-meal policy, based on certain local and perhaps political demands made upon the minister and based upon those alone. I appeal to the members of this committee on both sides. It is our duty as a committee to insist that this matter should be dealt with in a different manner. I do not often talk on the estimates, but I wish to enter my protest as earnestly as I can against the manner in which we have been proceeding.

Since the hon. minister has promised so much to my hon. friend from Medicine Hat, I would like to put on record the fact that Lethbridge has eleven banks, that the value of goods which have passed customs at that port of entry was last year $800,000 and the duties collected thereon $136,000.

It is a very important town and is growing very rapidly. ,
St. Lambert public building, $10,000.

This is to make pro-', vision for the construction of a public building to be used chiefly for post office purposes. There has been a petition signed by influential inhabitants of the town as early as March, 1907. This came to the Post Office Department first and was transmitted by the deputy Postmaster General to the Minister of Public Works. It is represented, I have no doubt correctly, that St. Lambert is rapidly increasing in population, having doubled in ten years, and that it is a town with all the modern improvements -waterworks and a sewerage system-and is going ahead very rapidly.
What is the population?
Nine years ago, according to the census, it was 1,362; but that is no criterion of what it is to-day.

The minister ought really to have that information in definite form.
Mr.' PUGSLEY. I do not carry in my pocket information as to the population of all these places.
The minister's first duty is to give us information as to the number of people to be served.

I can only give the hon. gentleman the population according to the last census. I am not supposed to go and take a census of these places from year to year. The population of St. Lambert today is probably from 2,000 to 2,500. The revenue last year was $2,615, and the year before it was $1,756.
What has the site cost?
It has not been purchased yet.
What is the estimated cost of the building and site?
Not exceeding $20,000.
Have the plans been prepared?
No.
No plans, no estimate, no statement of population?
In whose riding is this?
Chambly and Vercheres, represented by Mr. Geoffrion.
What is the salary?
And what is the present rental?

One would naturally expect that when the Minister of Public Works is submitting his estimates to Council, for the consideration of that body, he would supply them with better data than he furnishes this House to justify council in passing the estimates. There does not seem to be any system whereby he can reach a conclusion regarding the absolute need of buildings or the wisdom or otherwise of erecting buildings in these places. He has a request from somebody and cannot tell us. in some cases, from whom Not from the Post Office Department, the Post Office Department does not seem to give him any information whether there is a need for a public building or not. He does not seem to go to the trouble of making any inquiries from the Post Office Department or from any other source as to what the population of the place is or what its needs are. In defending the building of a post office costing about $20,000 in one place he said that it was on a railway. He could find places of three, four, or five times the size and importance of that place on railways all over this country that have no nublic buildings and no post offices erected by the government. I think that is no justification at all and no information.

["It is necessary for me to give some explanation. I thought the hon. gentleman spoke of the ' Acadia ' which is a very small boat. We do not consider this as anything more than an ordinary boat, a boat that runs along the coast and if we have to build a breakwater at Ingonish costing $30,000 for the accommodation of a boat that might run there once a week or

once a fortnight it is quite a large sum to pay for the service which we would receive. It is a serious matter for us in Nova Scotia where we have a great deal to do with the small amount of money that is spent. We think of our province as the wharf of Canada jutting away out into the Atlantic ocean and therefore we require a great deal. The province of Nova Scotia has done much for the west and for other parts of Canada. There is not a harbour in that province that does not.require some expenditure in the line of providing breakwater accommodation for the fishermen. Therefore, I was anxious that this sum should be divided up amongst some of the other ports. I have no objection at all if the government are willing to spend $30,000 for the accommodation of a very small steamer which will run perhaps not more than once a week or once a fortnight to Ingonish. I think it is not fair to other parts of the province of Nova Scotia which are really in need of breakwaters and wharfs, and which will continue to be in need of them as everybody knows in that part of the country.
