Before recess, we were at the item for a post office building at St. Lambert, which, I think, I explained very fully. I might, however, add that the present post office accommodation there is very poor. The postal service is transacted in a small grocery store with little or no accommodation for the people waiting for their mails, and there has been a very strong request from the people of that locality for a suitable building.
How did the hon. gentleman happen to get that information?
From a petition of the inhabitants.

Is that the way in which he usually gets his information regarding the necessity of a public building in any locality? In my part of the country, whenever the public need demands anything in the post office line, we usually apply to the Postmaster General, and one would naturally expect that he would be better posted on the matter than the Minister of Public Works. The Minister of Public Works has no one to rely on. He may have the member for the constituency, and it would be natural to expect that he would urge the requirements of his constituency as strongly as possible. In other cases he may have the defeated candidate, who may not happen to be in the locality and may pay very little attention to it. It would be natural therefore to expect that there would be some communication to the Postmaster General from the locality and that the minister would look to him for information. Take the Public Works Department, when a public work has to be done in connection with harbours and rivers, the department usually sends its own engineer to examine the locality; and if the department desires to get information regarding postal matters, it can call on the post office inspector to examine and report; but in none of these cases has the minister said he applied to the inspector for information to know whether the public building asked for is needed or not. What is the result? We have items in the estimates for the building of post offices in small places where there is little or no revenue and larger places are neglected, and in those small places buildings are provided at a cost out of all proportion to the needs of the locality. It seems to me that the minister ought to have some businesslike system by means of which he could obtain reliable information which he could submit to council and afterwards to the House in justification of the proposed expenditure.

I thought that before recess I had shown clearly the needs of this town for a public building. The place in the last eight years has about doubled its population. Its population is given by the directory to-day as 2,500. It is a very important suburb of Montreal. A large number of very fine residences have been erected in it, and the present post office accommodation is utterly inadequate. I did not depend solely on this petition but made inquiry of the sitting member who at first did not say he would urge it at present, but I asked him to look into the matter further, and give me his more matured judgment. After he bad been to St. Lambert, he urged very strongly that I should comply with the request of the petitioners. The building will not cost more than $25,000 at the outside. It will be a substantial structure which ought to serve the wants of the people there for the next half century, and I do not think I am asking any extravagant amount. With regard to consulting the Post Office Department, my hon. friend rightly says that, in respect of post office matters, the people generally communicate with the Postmaster General or his department. Speaking in a general way that is true. But that remark applies to postal services such as the establishment of additional post offices, and the giving of increased accommodation. I venture to say that not once in a hundred times do the people, when they desire a public building erected for a post office, apply directly to the Postmaster General, they make their application to the Department of Public Works. That has been my experience, and it is then my duty to get the best information 1 can as to the need of that work, and I do not know of any more reliable source to which I can apply than the sitting member for the county. When my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Owen) told me of the population and needs of Campbellford, I felt that I could rely on his statement, as I feel I can rely on the statement of any other member of this House.

I am not opposing this expenditure, I am only speaking in general terms with reference to what principle the Department of Public Works adopts in determining whether these buildings are required or not. The minister said he depends on the member. I do no.t object to that. But there are many places where there is no supporter of the government, and he does not seem to rely quite as much on the information he gets from an opposition member as he does on that he gets from a supporter of his own side. But I was speaking more particularly with regard to the general principle. Take the case we dealt with before six o'clock, a proposal to expend $20,000 in a village where the

revenue is only $700. I gave to the House a list of cases in a radius of, perhaps, less than 100 miles, in a locality with which_ I am well acquainted, where there are villages and towns much larger than this, and where the revenue was ten dimes as great, and yet there was no effort displayed on the part of the Minister of Public Works; to serve the needs of the public in these places. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the principle which guides the Minister of Public Works is not the urgent needs of the people. I do not think he can justify these expenditures in so many instances in the province of Quebec and so few in the province of Ontario.
Just as many in Ontario.

I do not think so, but I have not verified it. He cannot justify passing by so many places like Lethbridge, and other places in the west and in Ontario, where, notwithstanding every effort on 'the part of the people to get better accommodation, it has been heartlessly refused them; whereas in other places where the people scarcely asked for it, it has been given them. Now the minister says that when people want additional postal service and the like of 'that, they apply to the Post Office Department, but not in the matter of buildings. Now I know, speaking from long experience, that the very reverse of what the minister says is the case. Over and over again, in my own constituency and in others, have I been consulted, written to and urged by the people who told me that they had communicated with the Posit Office Department and could get no satisfaction.
Three Rivers-new public building-to replace buildings destroyed by fire, June 22, 1908, $60,000.

This is to provide for a new post office and customs building in the city of Three Rivers to replace those that were destroyed in the great fire. We have been using a _ temporary building in the meantime, but we think the time has now arrived when we should begin the erection of a new and permanent building. The appropriation for 1909-10 was $40,000. Of that, however, we only expended $10,000 to provide temporary quarters; so $30,000 is a revote, and we are now asking for an additional $30,000. This amount of $60,000 will be sufficient to enable us to enter into a contract for the construction of the building. We estimate it will probably cost somewhere from $125,000 to $150,000 when the building is entirely completed.
Quebec province-immigrant buildings generally, $5,000.

I would ask the committee to go back to this item in regard to Mr. SPROULE.
which the hon. member for North Toronto asked some explanations before recess. I mentioned that in addition 'to those at the city of Montreal and the city of Quebec, there was an immigrant building at, I think, Peribonka, Nominingue and, I think, Temiskaming. The question was asked as to -the principle upon which these small immigrant buildings were erected, and now that the Minister of the Interior is present, I thought he might make some statement.
What kind of immigrants do 'the government provide for at Nominingue?
Ordinary immigrants. I may say to my hon. friend that there is an immigration society which is working quite industriously in bringing immigrants into that locality and settling them upon 'the land.
The only settlers there are from the province of Quebec. They are not, as I understand, from outside.
I think my hon. friend is mistaken, because there is a considerable repatriation.
From where?

From the United States into the northern parts of Quebec. This work is carried on by one of the immigration societies formed in Quebec, which societies are subsidized by the government for that express purpose.
So much the better.
If these societies are paid for that work, what is the necessity of the government erecting buildings for them? Is it for the accommodation of the immigrants?
Certainly.
How many would be brought in at a time?
I cannot say as to that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The immigrants are not brought in, they come in of their own accord.
I thought the society was bringing them in.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The society employs special means of bringing the attractions of a special district before the immigrant. The government's business is to bring the advantages of the country at large before the immigrant, but the society is organized for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the immigrant a certain district, and that is the business of the societies that my hon. friend (Mr. Fisher) has alluded to.
What aTe the buildings that are used for this purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are, first, the Quebec immigration building on the Louise embankment; second, the Detention Hospital erected in 1907 at a cost of $75,000; third, the immigration building at Montreal, which serves the purposes of a hospital and immigration quarters, on St. Antoine street, and which costs $3,000 rental per annum. Then, there is the immigration building at Nominingue. This is a shelter for immigrants, the building being 45 by 27 feet 10 inches, and being the property of the government. This building is at the point which was the terminus of a branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway system and was the distributing point for immigrants in the northern part of Labelle. It was built for the purpose of giving accommodation for these settlers at the end of their railway journey before setting out for their locations in the surrounding country. In this building, and for the accommodation of the settlers, the Quebec government have their local land agent. The building contains four large rooms, two downstairs and two upstairs with cooking stoves, so that the immigrants have the advantage of being able to rest and cook during the time that they are preparing to go on their locations. There is an immigration building at Roberval, in the Lake St. John district, or a shelter for immigrants, the dimensions of which building are 60 by 30. The conditions are the same as in the case of Nominingue. There is the Peribonka immigration building, also in the Lake St. John district, for the same purpose. The dimensions are 45 by 25. This is the list of immigration buildings in the province of Quebec.
_ Mr. NANTEL. Is the minister in a position to give the cost of the building in Nominingue?
I cannot do so to-night, because the amount we are asking for is simply for repairs for the different immigration buildings in the province as a whole, but I will get it and lay it on the table.
Is the building used for post office purposes or only for immigration?
Only for immigration.

I would like to ask the minister whether he knows anything with regard to the report which appears in the press to the effect that several thousand Doukhobors are coming to our country in the near future and whether they are likely to be received?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no knowledge of any such movement, and I have no belief that any such movement is likely to take place.	*
Has the , minister any information as to the number of immigrants who have come into these localities within the last few years?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The estimates under consideration are those of the Public Works Department, and I am not able to give my hon. friend the information at the present time, but when the immigration estimates are up, and I have the assistance of the officers of the department, I hope to be able to give my hon. friend an answer.

I -would like to ask the minister if it is the policy of the government to erect these immigration buildings in all of the provinces for local needs? I thought that would rather be an expenditure * which would be expected from the provincial governments. Do they do that in other provinces where immigration work is carried on by the provincial authorities?
Yes. it has been done in other parts of Canada, for instance, I think in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
But these have been under the direct control of this federal government all the time?
Well, the Dominion is just as much interested in securing immigrants for the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces-
But you do not put up any buildings in these provinces?

-as it is in securing immigrants for. the west with the exception that it has land in the west. Still, to the ordinary settler, that land is given away upon the ordinary homestead conditions but even then the federal government is just as much interested in getting immigrants into the eastern provinces as it is in getting them into the western provinces. It is not undesirable to take care of the immigrants when they arrive in a new and unsettled district and make them as reasonably comfortable as you can until they set out for the land which they are going to occupy. There seems to be a considerable immigration into .the Lake St. John district and to the westward. There has been quite an extensive movement in the way of repatriation from the United States and I think that the small amount of money which has been expended upon these immigrant buildings has been very well expended and certainly has been productive of good results.

I am nut complaining of the amount of money which has been spent there. I am only asking what is the general principle, if it is the principle to erect these buildings in the different provinces, or have the provinces been doing this work themselves? There is a good deal of immigration going into the northern



part of Ontario, but I am not aware that the government has gone to the trouble of erecting immigration buildings to accommodate those who go there. The minister says that we have done tms in the northwest. There is good reason why we should do it there because we practically owned that country until the new provinces were established. Are there any other provinces where this is being done except that which the minister has referred to to-night? We should do the best we can for the immigrants who come to our shores, and I am not complaining if this is to be a general policy, but I was not aware that the federal government provided accommodation for immigrants brought here under the auspices of the different provinces.
We have immigration buildings in all the provinces, in Halifax, St. John, Montreal.
But these are sea-port towns.

What difference does it make in principle whether the immigrants come by train or by steamer; should we not provide accommodation for them? _ I can quite conceive that an immigrant building in the Lake St. John district from which the immigrants are distributed may do as effective work as an immigrant building in St. John or Halifax.
There is a good deal of immigration into the Cobalt district; would a proposition to erect an immigration building there be entertained by the minister?

If the immigrants were sent to Cobalt and distributed thence through that northern country and it would be desirable to house them comfortably, I think such a proposition might be entertained. For instance, we have an immigration building at Port Arthur.
That again is a sea-port and immigrants come to it by water and by rail.
The object is to make the immigrant comfortable until he gets located, and it does not make any difference by what means of transportation he arrives.

I see all the difference in the world between providing a building for immigrants at Port Arthur whence the immigrants are distributed all over the country, and providing a building at Lake St. John.
Westmount Public Buildings, $25,000.
Westmount is a very important suburb of Montreal, and this vote is asked to make provision for the purchase of a site and towards the erection of a post office building. It will be known as the St.

Catharines Street West Postal Station. It will be admitted that the building to be erected in Westmount should be of a substantial character and in keeping with the other handsome buildings in that city. The rent paid for the post office and letter carriers' depot last year was $1,200; the postal revenue was $9,131.43; money orders issued, $41,330, and money orders paid, $10,791. We have not prepared the plans as yet, nor purchased the site, but I should think that the site and building, all complete, will cost somewhere in the vicinity of $100,000.
What is the population of Westmount?
I understand that two or three years ago it was 11,000, but West-mount has grown rapidly and the population is now estimated at 15,000.

I do not think it is quite as large as that. I understand that in some of the smaller cities of from 10,000 to 12,000 population the post office has practically been closed, only a small portion of it being used for the purpose of getting the mail matter ready for the carriers. That brings up the question whether we should expend such a large amount of money on a post office in a small city.

If what the hon. gentleman says is the case, it is a matter for the post office authorities to consider. But I am not aware that the establishment of free delivery in any city has been the means of doing away with the post office or lessening the business done there. This building is going to be a centre from which the mail will be distributed over all that western part of Montreal.

I understand that Westmount is a part of Montreal or will ultimately be brought within the city; and if so, the postal business will be done through the general post office, this building will become a sub-station, and should not cost more than $15,000 or $20,000.
What is this building expected to cost?

I would like to ask the hon. minister how many of these expenditures in the nrovince of Quebec, covering about 40 items, are in constituencies represented by members on the opposition side. I ask this question because this afterneon we were endeavouring to ascertain the policy of the minister as to the expenditure of public money. .

If my hon. friend will tell meliow many opposition members there

are from the province of Quebec and in what constituencies there are demands for public buildings, I will give him the in-.formation. I think my hon. friend is not serious, because he can tell as well as I. For instance, there are expenditures at Lachine, at Sherbrooke, in the city of Montreal and in the city of Quebec. So if my hon. friend counts them, I think he will find that they are doing pretty well, considering their numbers.

Perhaps a little more specific answer would be more satisfactory to the committee. I understand there is a small item for repairing the post office in Sherbrooke. My hon. friend would not suggest that that is an expenditure of public money other than to keep up a building erected several years ago.
An absolutely necessary expenditure, like all the others.

I am not objecting to that. I am asking the minister to state how many expenditures for new buildings are to be made in counties represented on the opposition side. My hon. friend would be able I am sure, having all the information *before him, to give us an answer to that question.

I regret to say that I have not had that classified in that way and therefore I could npt just at this moment, give my hon. friend all the information, but really I do not think it is fair that my hon. friend should ask me. He knows that I am the target of a dozen or more of my hon. friends opposite; I have to answer legitimate and proper questions. My hon. friend is entirely a gentleman, at leisure just at the moment and he could make up the figures just as readily as I could, and he would be obliging me very much if he would do it himself.
That may be all right for my hon. friend the minister, but I do not think the committee will gather very much information from that statement.
They will take my hon. friend's statement.

Well, I will ask the minister to give an answer to the question with a list of the expenditures, and if my hon. friend is unable to do it now, he has a good many clerks in his department and perhaps it could be made up and submitted at a future sitting, if my hon. friend would say he would bring a list
No, I cannot say I would like to undertake that.

Perhaps he had better take it now.
