Does my hon. friend intimate that he is going to force me to do this? In what way does he propose to force it?
I have no thought in my mind of anything of the kind.
I am glad of that.

My hon. friend knows very well that we on this side are not anxious to force my hon. friend to do anything-he is doing too many things now without any suggestion from this side. I think it has been made clear that what the committee are anxious to know is whether it is the policy of the government to grant public buildings in all towns where there is a large revenue from the customs and postal service or if that is a policy that applies only to constituencies represented by supporters of my hon. friend. I thought my hon. friend would be glad of an opportunity to assure the committee that there was no partisanship in the expenditure of this money.

I think that before my hon. friend asks whether these improvements are in constituencies represented by Liberals or Conservatives, he ought to be able to show that in some case in the province of Quebec represented by a Conservative there has been a real necessity for some public work which I have refused. The only cases which have been referred to are those of Grand-Mere and Ste. Th6rese, and I explained that in these towns the public buildings have been allowed to stand over simply because I had no representations made to me before these estimates were prepared that public buildings were urgently required in those two places. This afternoon I was able to appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite representing constituencies in all parts of Canada as to whether or not I had discriminated against their constituencies and my hon. friend must rfemember that strong testimonly was borne to the fact by at least one gentleman on his side of the House-and I think if other hon. gentlemen had an opportunity they would bear like testimony-that their constituencies had been treated not generously, because we do_ not treat constituencies generously, but justly, that the reasonable requirements of the people had been met as far as their constituencies were concerned, and I do think, under these circumstances, that my hon. friend will see that it is not reasonable that he should take up the time of the committee by asking consideration of this matter. If my hon. friend wishes to point out where I have done any injustice to any constituency represented by a Conservative let him do so, but I am not aware of any such case.

967
I need not go very far to answer that. Take my own county, for example.
That is not Quebec, these are Quebec buildings that are under consideration.

I understand that, but my hon. friend knows that the statements made by the hon. gentlemen on this side were Erom other portions of Canada and not from Quebec at all. My hon. friend from Nipis-sing was the member to whom the minister particularly referred. That was not in Quebec. My own county is an example. My hon. friend's two immediate predecessors both stated in this Chamber that a very necessary expenditure of money in the county of Peel would be made. When I directed the attention of my hon. friend to that statement in ' Hansard,' my Iron, friend was not prepared to fulfil the pledges of his predecessors to this House, and to my constituency. I do not wish to make a personal matter of this. I am expecting, of course, that out of the fulness of my hon. friend's heart the work will be done this coming year, and therefore I shall not enter into any severe criticism of that matter.
Quebec Citadel-drill shed for school of gunnery, $16,000.

The object of this is to afford a school of gunnery for the whole Dominion in which lectures can be delivered and the use of every type of gun in Canada illustrated and taught. There will be lecture rooms for instruction on ammunition, coast defence, electricity, range, &c., a complete gunnery school.
Military Buildings-additional storage to ordnance stores, $5,000.
This is an additional story to the ordnance stores as requested by the Department of Militia and Defence, May 26, 1909.

This is simply additional accommodation absolutely required.
Quebec Military Buildings-additional storage to ordnance stores.

This is to provide additional accommodation for stores of every kind. There is a large storage building in Quebec, but it has become too small. The stores there are issued as required in different parts of the country. In many respects perhaps next to Ottawa, and in some respects larger than in Ottawa, stores of the Dominion are lodged there. In particular there is a much larger quantity of rifles stored in Quebec than any where else.
Is the building fire-proof?
I hope the new part will be at least.
What is the capacity of stores buildings in Quebec t
10,000 square feet.
What is the total capacity for storage in the city of Quebec for military purposes?
I could not say just now but will get the information.
Have tenders been asked for?
We have not started this yet, but of course will call for tenders.
Are any buildings provided for military purposes without requisition from the Militia Department?
No
Why is that rule not adopted in the case of the post offices and customs houses?
Because that never has been the rule, and the conditions are entirely different.

I do not see that they are. It seems most extraordinary that the Minister of Public Works should go on spending money erecting post offices and customs houses in different constituencies without any report from the Post Office or Customs Department that such buildings are required. I should think that a new practice ought to be adopted and that in every case there should be a requisition from the department for whose use the building is provided, and such requisition should set- forth the necessity for it.
Are the stores under the care of the Ordnance Stores Department and are they for the use of the permanent corps or active militia?

All the stores are issued from the same building. The stores, both for the permanent force and active militia, are put in this building. I believe the stores are entirely under the control of the ordnance store corps except in so far as some police protection naturally would be given by the city authorities.
Are the stores there under the same supervision as here in Ottawa ?
Yes.
No insurance?
No.
No watchman?
Yes, there are watchmen.

The care taken seems to be of very imperfect character. In Ottawa by one fire we lost $120,000 in stores and $30,000 in damage to the building. There was neither insurance, nor regular watchmen who visited the building at stated periods in twenty-four hours.

The government never in suae but simply follow the rule which has been followed in every department since confederation. The $30,000 loss was caused by damage to the building, and I hope that the loss in clothing will not amount to $120,000. Some of the clothing, I might mention, was clothing which would not have been issued again.
Let me remind the hon. gentleman that I put a question, on the paper as to whether this $120,000 worth of goods was a total loss, and his answer was yes.

I understand that the damage to the building was $30,000 and the damage to the clothing $120,000. As to whether proper precaution was taken that might be a matter of opinion, but we believe that we were taking proper precautions, and it was understood that the building was fire-proof. I have had a careful investigation made, and when the time comes I propose to make a statement to the House. But I may mention that the result of the investigation went to show that the fire resulted from a defective electric wire.
What is the value of the new clothing in the building?
Is it not a fact that the regulations of the ordnance stores department require that where a large quantity of stores are kept, it is necessary to keep a military guard at night?
No.

I think that the consensus of opinion of good business men would be that there ought to be some insurance in the case of valuable property stored. It seems to me that would be money well invested. Only a short time ago a portion of the legislative buildings in Toronto was burnt down. The present government there did what this government might do to good purpose. When they came into power they found that there was no insurance on the building; they put an insurance on it, and now they have something to fall back upon in the way of insurance; otherwise there would not have been a dollar to help replace the building that was burned. Would it not be better for the minister to consider
making a new departure, and to provide, either insurance, or better care by watchmen?

I agree that that is a fair question for investigation and inquiry. It would be necessary to carry the inquiry over a good many years, and to see what amount of property would be risked in this way, what the actual losses have been, and what it would cost to insure the buildings. I think that is a very desirable thing to do.
Do I understand that the total value of the clothing destroyed was $900,000?
No, the total amount in the building was $900,000, of which about $120,000 was destroyed. I misunderstood the hon. gentleman's question.

A question arises in connection with this fire which I think the minister should seriously consider. The equipment and clothing of most of the militia men in Canada is kept in a stores building at Ottawa. In case war or trouble of any kind should occur, it would take three or four weeks to get that clothing out of this central depot and distribute it all over the country. Should not the minister consider, when we are building barracks or drill sheds in various places, whether the policy of decentralization would not be better in regard to these stores than the present system under which the country has lost $120,000? It has often been a subject of comment by military men, that if they wanted a pair of trousers, or a Glengarry, for one of their men 200 miles away, they had to send along a requisition and that has to come from Ottawa. Under the system that obtains in other countries, every district is eauipped with its own stores, its own ammunition, its own rifles, it is a complete unit by itself, and is capable of taking the field armed inside of two or three days. Under no system could this clothing be distributed from Ottawa in case of war, and sent to the various quarters inside of four or five weeks. It seems to me that the old policy of the department of centralizing everything at Ottawa in order that somebody may have a ]ob of overlooking it, is at the bottom of this, and when we get to the bottom of the whole thing, we find there is1 nobody looking after it when it takes fire. These stores might just as well have been at Toronto, at Kingston, at Esquimalt, distributed equitably amongst them in that way, and then in case of emergency the stores could be got out in two or three days.
Sir FREDERICK BORDriN. I do not think it desirable to enter into this discussion now very fully. But I may tell mv hon. friend that he is quite mistaken if he

supposes that all the stores are here in Ottawa, that is not the case.
I did not say that.

It is true that the reserve stores are here. But I quite agree with him that it would be desirable to distribute these stores more than they are distributed now, and that is our intention. Unfortunately at the present time we have not a suitable building, and we have been unable to get one. We are now occupying some buildings rented before this fire, a year ago, a large building in Montreal and one in Toronto, and it is intended to distribute the stores more than they have been. My hon. friend refers to other countries. Well, this country, for instance, compared with!, the mother country, is a country of magnificent distances; and while in England the stores are kept pretty much together, and possibly we might have been governed to some extent by that fact, we must remember that the centres in Canada are widely distributed, and it will be necessary for us to have several centres of distribution. At the present" time we keep a certain amount of stores in Winnipeg, considerably more than the usual quantity; nearly all the saddlery stores are in Toronto, and there are stores at London, some at Kingston, some in Mont-treal, a large auantity; there are stores in Halifax, in Quebec, and on the Pacific coast. I agree that the point raised by the hon. gentleman is worthy of consideration.
Is the ammunition distributed in such a way that it can be got at?
Yes.
I understand there is a small quantity stored at various points; but what proportion of ammunition is centralized and what proportion is at Ottawa?

That is a question which I think my hon. friend, being a military man himself, must understand is not one that it is desirable to answer. That question has been raised more than once, and the answer I have given is that if any hon. gentleman, a member of this House, will come to my office, I will be glad to tell him the distribution of the ammunition. But I do not think it is desirable to publish to the world exactly how the ammunition in Canada is distributed.

That is like the right hon. gentleman when an embarrassing question is asked him; he takes refuge by saying: If you ask me privately I will tell you this, that, or the other thing. Let me tell the Minister of Militia that in the mother country a government was upset on Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
this question of ammunition. The question was brought up in the House of Commons, and the minister had to answer that he had not sufficient ammunition to meet the country's needs, and the government was thrown out of office. Questions of this kind must be answered in some place where the people will know. The minister says he will answer me privately how this ammunition is distributed. I am not asking how many cartridges he has at various points, but if he has inaugurated a fair system of distribution, in order to avoid the abuse that has occurred where, when a man requires a shell, he has to wire to Ottawa to get it.
I don't think that is the case.

The minister says that questions of this kind have been asked several times in the House. I asked the other day something about Hie stores on the Great Lakes, and I received the same answer. Now, as my hon. friend from Sim-coe (Mr. Currie) says, you can always find out these things in the United Kingdom. You can go most anywhere and buy a little manual for one and six and find out where the different stores are. I do not see any objection in giving the information to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To return to the question of insurance, particularly to what has been said by the hon. member for East Grey as to the good luck that the Ontario government had in having its building insured at the time of the fire. It might be a wise and proper policy for a provincial government to insure its property, and not necessarily a wise policy for the Dominion government to do so. From my own experience in the provincial government, it seemed desirable that we should carry a large amount of insurance. But in every large business the principle is adopted that, as you increase the volume of your property, the need of insurance in a certain sense diminishes. A man can afford to insure for himself, but the steamship people who have a large number of vessels do not find it advantageous to do so. If a man has only one or two vessels, he may insure them; but those who are fortunate enough to have a dozen vessels, in many cases do not insure; they simply open an insurance account; and they have found that, take it all in all, they were making a profit by not taking their business to the companies. I am not saying the province of Ontario was not wise, and from my own experience in the provincial government, I believed in carrying an insurance. But when you have the vast volume of property which the Dominion government has, stretched over the whole continent, it might be the best policy

not to insure. That seems to have been the policy of all the governments in Canada.
I am bound to say the fact that we occasionally have a fire does no't by any means prove that that policy is a mistake.

If the government had gone into a calculation to determine whether, from their experience of the last 50 years, it would be better not to insure, I could understand such an argument. But this day and age, when insurance is so very reasonable in cities and towns, where you have good fire protection, waterworks and fireproof buildings, it seems to me that it is doubtful wisdom'to have great stores of supplies in any building without being insured. I would at least expect that the government would be in a position to present the House with some data which would justify that conclusion. If they have not got it, I think it would not be amiss for them to take the earliest opportunity to make some such calculation. I think the experience of most business people would be that it is not the part of wisdom to allow large collections of property to remain anywhere without some insurance, or some better protection, than that which we had for the military clothing and supplies thait are stored in Ottawa, Quebec and elsewhere

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So far as protection is concerned, I am with my hon. friend when he says that the government is bound to see that every possible care is taken for the protection of its property. I do not differ from him on that. If there be a large volume of property accumulated at one centre where the risk is very great, certainly it calls for insurance, but where you have the same volume of property distributed over a wide area the risk is reduced to a small figure and I do not think it needs any calculation to justify the noninsurance of such property. It is a principle that where your property is widely distributed you can just as well insure it yourself as any insurance company could do it. It might be a matter of convenience and of curiosity to make a statement, but a government is not bound to do it to the same extent as a private corporation. Even if a big fire burned down these magnificent parliament buildings I do not think it would necessarily prove that the policy of the administration is wrong.
Assuming that we have $50,000,000 worth of property belonging to the government and that the average insurance rate would probably be one per cent, there would be $500,000 a year.
Oh, the average insurance rate would not amount to that.

Put it at one-half per cent, which is very low; there is $250,000 a year. I doubt if, in the forty-two years
since confederation, there has been a million dollars worth of property destroyed, whereas the insurance premiums would have amounted to a great deal more than that. As my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance said, it is purely a question of the amount of property you have. The experience of our St. John ship-owners is just the same as that of those to whom my hon. friend refers in Nova Scotia. These firms, owning a large number of vessels, never thought of insuring their vessels because it would be cheaper to lose a ship ocasionally than to pay the premiums. If we could tell when a fire was going to occur and insure just before it took place it would be all right, but we should have to take the insurance year by year and it would cost a great deal more, as experience since confederation has shown, than the fire losses would amount to.

The minister says that there might have been a loss of a million dollars since confederation. Why, two or three years ago we had a loss of a good portion of a million dollars when the fire in the west block occurred. Then, take the fire which occurred in the militia stores building when $120,000 worth of clothing was entirely destroyed and $30,000 damage was done to other clothing, not entirely destroyed, besides the loss to the building. These are only two fires out of others which could be mentioned. But then the same principles would apply to a private corporation or to the government. Would any business man in this country follow out the same principle in dealing with his own private business?
Ship-owners do it constantly.

I am not familiar with their business, therefore I do not know, but the argument that because the risks are distributed amongst a large number of centres reduces the need for insurance I do not think carries any weight at all, because a man worth $10,000,000 having property distributed all over the continent insures on the same principle as though he had it only in one province. He regards that as a good business principle, and it is generally recognized as a good one.
But the loss is lessened by the distribution of the property?

It may be lessened to a certain extent by distribution of property, but if it is lessened the insurance will cost less. Take the mill owners, factory men or merchants who are handling produce or cattle-they all insure, but the government do not think it wise to insure. I do not think they can give any data to justify them in reaching that conclusion.

I think there is quite a difference between the Dominion government insuring its property, scattered ail over the broad Dominion, and the case of a private party insuring his property whether it be a large or a small property. An insurance company, calculating its rates and business, expects to reach an average rate of loss and be able to fix, on that average, the premium it should collect. The Dominion government has so much property scattered all over the Dominion that it will reach about the same average of loss that the insurance company will and that being the ease the government, in doing without insurance, saves the commissions paid to agents, office management of the insurance company and all the profits that the insurance company expects to receive.
Mr. SPRObkE. If the hon. gentleman's argument is worth a cent it applies to insurance in every line, whether there is one centre or a dozen, because every man who insures pays for carrying the risk and pays a profit to the party who is carrying it whether it is upon a barn in the country or a factory in the city. If it applies to the government property that may be distributed in a hundred centres it applies on the same parity of reasoning to the property which is distributed in three centres, or is in one place.

Perhaps I have not made myself clear, but it would be utterly impossible that all the property of the government would be destroyed at or near the one time. Because of the law of average, the saving that through non-insurance will De effected at toe very many points where no losses occur will make un, or more than make un, the occasional losses of properties that do bum.
You might say that of any business.

Might I suggest to the minister that buildings containing valuable government property should be in the future built with a system of sprinklers and the protection called for by the insurance companies which reduces the risk, they claim, from about one per cent to one fifteenth of one per cent. * It does not add very much to the cost of the building and if the government is not going to carry any insurance it would be a very wise investment.

It is worthy of careful consideration.
Military Buildings-barrack accommodation for Canadian Permanent Army Service Corps, $8,000.
This is to provide accommodation for 25 officers, noncommissioned officers and men. These

troops have been stationed at Quebec during the last two years and no baracks have been available. They have been temporarily quartered at the Riding School. This vote is to provide new quarters for them. The proposed site is in the Cove Fields near the Riding School.
What is to be the cost of the building?
Harbours and Rivers, Nova Scotia-Annapolis harbour - improvements, ice piers, $15,000.

This matter was under discussion at considerable length last year and the minister gave a very fair statement to the committee so far as he was able at the time. Who has the contract, what is the amount of the contract, and does the minister believe that the work will be satisfactory in fulfilling its purpose?

The contract was first awarded to Messrs. Reid and Archibald for $34,400, but they declined to sign the contract as drawn by the department because it made them responsible for the work during construction. New tenders were called for and three tenders were received, ranging from $46,736 to $47,000. The lowest tender was that of the Nova Scotia Construction Company, Limited, and the contract was awarded to them. Their tender was a little above the chief engineer's estimate, which, was $45,625. The work is going on satisfactorily and it is expected that this amount will complete the payments to the contractors. The work is designed to resist tne flow of the ice coming down the river and so keep the harbour of Annapolis open all the year round.
Is it the intention to connect these piers with any superstructure?
It is not the present intention.
Is it intended to do so in the future?
No; it is not like the wharfs at St. Genevieve that were referred to the other day.
It is not intended to make a bridge of it?
Not that I am aware of; it could not be.
Who are the officers of the Nova Scotia Construction Company?
The names are on the contract, but I have not the contract with me. I shall be glad to get the names if the hon. gentleman desires.

I should like to have them.

Arichat wharf, $10,000.
It is understood that the Plant line of steamers are going to make Arichat a nort of call when this wharf is completed. The total estimated cost is $25,000.
Is it the intention to have this work done by contract?
Yes.
Is there any policy in the department as to when work shall be done by contract and when by day work?

In all cases where the work can be as well done by contract as by day work we call for tenders, but where there is repairing to be done it can often better be done bv day work where you have a good foreman. However, we prefer to call for tenders whenever we can.
Black Point breakwater, $5,000.
Will this work be done by contract?
I think it will be, unless it should be better to do it by day work.
What would make it better?
It may be more economical. This is an out-of-the-way place, and it might be better to send a competent foreman to do the work.
Will this cover the whole cost?

No, we will require $3,300 more. The total cost of the work will be $8,300.
Blue Rocks Island-breakwater at western end, $5,000.

The total estimated cost of this work is $15,000.
Bluff Head-breakwater extension, $2,500.

This is to extend the breakwater 90 feet, recommended by the resident engineer. This amount it is expected will complete the work.
Breen's Pond-breakwater, $8,000.
This is to build a breakwater to provide shelter for fishing boats. The estimated cost is $14,000.
Will tenders be asked for this work?
Yes.
The minister mentioned that the Bluff Head breakwater extension had been recommended by the resident engineer. Do I understand that such a recommendation is peculiar to that item alone?

Oh, no. My memorandum happened to be to that effect. The course pursued with regard to all works is that when an application is made, it is referred to the chief engineer for the purpose of obtaining a report from the resident engineer as to the public necessity which exists for the work, the extent of traffic which will be accommodated or the protection which will be given, and the estimated cost of the work.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the wharf or pier at Parrsboro is in a very bad condition. The planks upon it are so rotten that horses and carriages cannot go on it with safety. Parrsboro is an important point, not only as a railway terminus, but because there is a daily steamship service between that point and Canning in the county of Kings. The condition of the wharf has been a serious matter to the ship-owners this year. The repairs would not cost much, as there is on the wharf a large quantity of plank owned by the department which could be used for the purpose. I brought the matter to the attention of the minister and the deputy minister some time ago, and was informed that it would be referred to the resident engineer for a report.

Direction was given some time ago to have a report made on the wharf at Parrsboro. I do not at this moment remember what the report was, but the matter will receive consideration. It may be that the work can be done out of the general vote for repairs.

I inspected this wharf personally last summer and I think $50 for labour, with the material on hand, would put the wharf in repair. It is very urgently needed.
Brooklyn-towards reconstruction of breakwater, $25,000.
This is not a new work, but it is to rebuild a work which was constructed a good many years ago, and which has gone to considerable decay.

In this connection I wish to mention the landing wharf at Cen-treville. This work is not only in the interest of the people of that locality, but in the interest of the department itself. As I am informed, owing to the fact that the toredo has eaten off the lower end of the piling, the whole work is in danger of collapsing in any heavy storm. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister by correspondence, and he informed me that it would be put into the hands of the engineer for inquiry. Has the minister ascertained just what the state of the work is, and if so, will steps be taken to protect

it at an early date in order that the work will not he entirely destroyed? The work itself is not sufficient to furnish the facilities required by that place. It was constructed prior to confederation and lengthened twelve or fifteen years ago and a comparatively small expenditure of $500 or $600 was made later. A prosperous settlement has developed there and the business now warrants much greater harbour facilities than are available. A steamboat makes connection with St. John, and there is perhaps the largest manufacuring plant for the putting up of fish in the county of Digby. Many hundreds of people are absolutely dependent on the industry prosecuted within the protection of this particular harbour. If the wharf or breakwater were extended, or indeed if a new structure were built, as I believe will be necessary, further to the right of the present structure, a much larger business would develop there. But in the meantime it is absolutely necessary that some work should be done to protect the present structure from destruction.

As there is no item in the estimates for the wharf at Centreville, I have no memorandum with me about it, but I shall look the matter up and give my hon. friend the information later on. I regret that I have not the information.
Brule wharf-repairs and extension, revote of lajjsecl amount, $2,200.

This is for repairs and extension of the wharf at Brule. This is the total estimated cost.
Burk's Head or Robert's Cove, North In-gonisk-breakwater, $28,500.

This Is the total estimated cost of this breakwater. It is to be 300 feet in length with an ' L ' on the outer end, 75 feet long. It will have to be heavily built as it is exposed to severe gales, and the full sweep of the Atlantic.
What accommodation will this afford and how many vessels or ships will be accommodated by it?
Perhaps my hon. friend from Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) who is personally familiar with the situation could give the most satisfactory information

The breakwater at Burke's Head is required like the few breakwaters we have along North Victoria for the purpose of protecting the fishermen. We have at Ingonish, North Bay and South Bay a large settlement of fishermen who are entirely dependent for their living upon fishing. The coast is exposed to the full swing of the Atlantic, and when it is blowing at all they cannot go out or come in without something in the shape of a breakwater. The making of a harbour is Mr. JAMESON.
out of the question and this protection is absolutely necessary. This breakwater has been asked for many years to create a shelter behind which boats can run when coming in and where they can be moored at nights in safety even in a storm. Hon. members who are familiar with the use of breakwaters will not require any further information about it except that it is absolutely necessary for the protection of the fishermen, that without it they are suffering great loss. We are very pleased indeed that this vote is in the estimates. No hon. gentleman who is familiar with the needs of the fishermen will object to it.

I have no desire to object to it but I wish to know what accommodation it is going to afford to people in that end of the province. We require many breakwaters in Nova Scotia, our fishermen require a great deal of assistance, and I only wish to ascertain whether it is essential that we should spend so much money at that particular point or whether it would not be well to spend some in other ports. If the hon. gentleman would state whether there is any shipping there, we would have more information than we have at present.

It will serve as a wharf at which the steamboat now plying between North Sydney and North Victoria will call. It is impossible for the boat to call without a dock and the fishermen, in order to send out their fish and land supplies, have to run out a couple of miles to meet the steamboat. That is a very inconvenient and hazardous way of doing business and one which causes a great deal of loss to these men because they cannot make any definite contract to send away their fish as they have to depend entirely on weather conditions as to whether they can put their freight on board the steamer or not. This will enable the steamer to come in in all reasonable conditions of weather. I cannot promise that any large shipping will get shelter ttjere because to make a breakwater which would protect large vessels would involve much more expenditure than the comparatively small amount required here. It will, however, afford shelter to 50 or 60 boats that are fishing off there and to other boats from Neill's harbour or North shore which may be caught in bad weather when fishing off Ingonish.
What is the size of the steamer which this breakwater is to accommodate?

The ' Weymouth ' is the steamer doing the business now but I cannot tell her size. We are getting a new steamer called the 'Aspev', a very much larger boat, built recently at Shelburne and fitted out at Weymouth. My hon. friend may perhaps remember the 'Scotia' running between Halifax and somewhere

down in Guysboro. The 'Aspey' is largely on the lines of the 'Scotia' and a little larger.

Now that the Minister of Public Works has handed over his task to my hon. friend, we cannot fail to be convinced that there is no question of nolitics in this. I have no desire whatever to interfere with any estimate because the only trouble we have is that we have not sufficient money to go round, but when he says this breakwater is to accommodate a steamer of between ten and fifteen tons, one cannot help questioning the necessity for it.
I do not think my hon. friend would like to venture on the North Atlantic. along that coast in a ten ton steamer.
I know the steamer very well and he does not. She is not over fifteen tons, as he will find if he refers to the blue-book.
I am quite willing to have the records in the blue-books produced, and if so my hon. friend will find himself in a very ridiculous position. The ' Weymouth ' is seven times that capacity.
I did not understand there was more than one boat running to this place. When will this new boat commence running there?

There is only one boat making regular trips along that shore as there is not enough traffic for more than one. The 'Aspey' is taking the place of the 'Weymouth' which has been running there the last ten years, subsidized both by the Nova Scotia government and this government. She is getting to be old and not equal to_ the business, and a new boat has been built called the 'Aspey', but I do not think she is yet on the route. The hon. gentleman will find a nhotograph and description of her in the office of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. .
What is the tonnage of this new boat?
Not being a shipping man myself, I do not carry her dimensions in my mind, but my hon. friend can get all the details he requires from the Department of Trade and Commerce.

When the hon. gentleman says that the 'Weymouth' is only ten or fifteen tons, he cannot have ever seen her. She is five times that tonnage. I know the boat for she ran between Weymouth and Yarmouth a number of years.
How many feet of water does she draw?
About 8 feet and the new boat about 10 feet.
What is the depth of water at low tide?
That will depend on how far you run out the breakwater. This breakwater, when built will have a depth of water at low tide of ten feet to accommodate that boat.
We ought to know, before we vote to build a breakwater, how far out we shall have to build it and what are its dimensions.
I have said already that the breakwater is to be 300 feet in iength with an L on the western side 75 feet in length.

How comes it that in the province of Nova Scotia with a population of 450,000, you have 111 separate items in the estimates and are going to spend there just about the same amount as in Ontario with a population of 2,114,000, not including the city of Ottawa.

The principle which has guided me, is, as far as possible, to get appropriations for what seems to be necessary for public works which have been brought to my notice. The size of a province or its population is not always the governing factor as to the amount of money required to be expended there on wharfs and breakwaters. Ontario is a very large province but a great deal of it is inland and does not call for expenditures on wharfs. But when the hon. gentleman speaks of the amount being expended in Ontario, he forgets altogether the very large expenditure made in Toronto, amounting to something like $700,000, which alone overtops all the expenditures in all the harbours along the whole coast of Nova Scotia. He leaves out altogether also the expenditure of some $900,000 at Fort William and Port Arthur, which is $300,000 more than all the expenditures asked for upon harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia. He likewise omits the expenditures at Tiffin and Victoria Harbour, which together amount to one-half the total expenditures on wharfs and breakwaters in Nova Scotia, also the exDenditures at Collingwood and Goderich.
Do these appear under the heading of expenditure in the estimates for Ontario?
No, Tiffin and Victoria do not, Goderich does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows they are in Ontario, does he not?

Tiffin and Victoria are in capital account, and do not appear in these items, because there is no capital account for the province of Nova Scotia, whereas there are $1,200,000 for harbour im-

provements in the province of Ontario which are charged to capital account. You have in those three places alone twice as much as we are asking for in respect to all the harbours, breakwaters and wharfs in the province of Nova Scotia, and that leaves out altogether the large improvements going on in the city of Toronto.

Let the minister look at his own book in the matter of current expenditures, and he will find $684,000 is spent in the province of Ontario on current expenditure. While some of these ' other expenditures are being made in Ontario, the large ones have been made in the eastern provinces.
Look at page 55 and you will see the harbours in Ontario.
I am taking the items in Ontario, 44 items, and 111 separate iteips in the province of Nova Scotia. I merely ask the minister to explain that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has in his hands the estimate which shows that for harbours and rivers in the fresh water province of Ontario you have $1,262,000; while in the inland province of Nova Scotia out in the ocean, you have $600,000. Yet the hon. gentleman thinks it is too much.

I would like to say just a word here. Since I came to Ottawa I have heard in the corridors, and outside as well, this same remark made by some members from Ontario on both sides of the House. I think they forget the fact that every one of the 18 counties of Nova Scotia fronts on the sea, and it is necessary that these counties should be provided with wharfs. As a matter of fact, whichever government might be in power, I have no doubt that there will be misappropriations and male expenditures from time to time. But in any case it is necessary that these expenditures should be made, and there is no other body to make them but the Dominion government. I think it ill becomes members from the other provinces to criticise the small amount the province of Nova Scotia is getting, which is only a fair proportion of the amount expended on public works.
Mr. ARMSTRONG- I was just asking for my own information. If the hon. gentleman will look at the province of Ontario, he will see that there are a large number of counties fronting on the great lakes and on the river, and he will recognize that they have important wharfs to build and maintain. If the Minister of Finance had been here this afternoon he would have heard from a number of gentlemen from the province of Ontario who have been pleading with the Minister of Public Works for years, not only with this minister but Mr. PUGSLEY.
with his predecessors, begging him, I might almost say, to spend a small amount of money in making public works where they were really necessary. We know that he has been making expenditures in other parts of the country where they were not nearly as necessary as many of the towns mentioned this afternoon.

I do not believe the people of the great province of Ontario will justify my hon. friend in seeking to raise prejudice against one section with respect to these expenditures. He asked how it was that there was only the small sum of $600,000 being expended in similar works in Ontario, while there was about an equal amount being expended in Nova Scotia. But as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, for public works chargeable to income in the province of Ontario, the amount which we ask is $1,262,850, for harbours and rivers only, outside of public buildings altogether. To that is to be added the amounts found in page 55, $800,000 for harbour improvements in Port Arthur and Fort William, also in the province of Ontario, $120,000 for improvements at Tiffin harbour, in the province of Ontario, and $145,000 for improvements at Victoria harbour, also in Ontario. There you have altogether upwards of two million and a quarter dollars being expended in the inland province of Ontario for harbours and rivers alone.

I do not wish the minister to try to lead this House to believe that I am attempting to raise prejudice between the provinces. Of the amounts that he has mentioned, a large portion is for capital account.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What difference does it make?
I might say the same in Nova Scotia, a large portion, I suppose in Halifax would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nothing in capital account for 'harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia.
Possibly not this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia I do not recollect a dollar being voted on capital account.
For harbours and rivers in Ontario, has a dollar been voted on capital account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, here to-day my hon. friend has just shown you sums amounting to $2,000,000.
These were for special improvements such as were necessary on the Welland canal. You might as well call that harbours and rivers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is for the harbour of Fort William, the harbour of Port Arthur, the harbour of Collingwood, the harbour of Goderich. What are these but harbours?
Are they on capital account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Many of them. Tiffin and Victoria harbours and Fort William, these are all capital account, and there is not a dollar for capital account in the province of Nova Scotia, in that service.
Some of the harbours and rivers are, put into capital account and some into current account. Explain your system of book-keeping.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Large development works, such as the class of works in the river St. Lawrence, have for years been charged to capital account. They differ only in volume. The smaller works are usually charged to income account. The province has nothing to do with it.
Central Economy Wharf-renewal of stem -revote of $1,200 lapsed, $2,000.
What is the nature of the work?

Some four years ago this work .was damaged by ice, it had not been completely close piled. There was a heavy run of ice and the wharf was damaged, and it required to be repaired. I may say the stem of the wharf at a distance of 120 feet from the shore was lifted by the ice, and the crib-work abutment at the shore end was undermined.
Chapel Cove Breakwater-revote of $3,000 lapsed, $5,000.

This is for a breakwater 240 feet in length and twenty feet wide on
top.	It is to be constructed partially of creosoted timber. The estimated cost is $7,800.
David's Cove Breakwater-wharf extension, $4,300.
This is for the purpose of extending the breakwater and is urgently required.
Will that work be done by contract?
I think this will probably be done by day labour, but we have not decided.

I know the locality and the people there and I would like to suggest to the minister that tenders should be asked and that if possible the work should be done by contract. I think it could be done more satisfactorily for a variety of reasons. I think the department will get much better value for the expenditure, and that the people would be better satisfied.

That matter will be carefully considered.
Deep Brook-pile wharf-revote of $500 lapsed, $1,500.	*

This is to make provision towards constructing a substantial wharf and pile work about 200 feet long with a return at the outer end, giving a frontage of 150 feet. It will cost about $3,500. We will have probably next year to ask for a further vote, but $1,500 is all we require this year.
Delap's Cove Breakwater-part reconstruction of shore end-revote of $800, lapsed, $1,000.

This is to complete the reconstruction of a portion, being about half, of the shore end block of the breakwater at this place. This will finish the work.
Delorey's Beach, Monk's Head-breakwater -revote of $4,000, lapsed, $6,500.

This is to complete the breakwater which is 300 feet long.
Devil's Island-breakwater-extension of- revote of $4,800, lapsed, $6,000.

This is to provide for the extension of Devil's island breakwater with an arm at the outer end. The object is to provide a shelter for motor and other boats of the fishermen. There is a large fishing industry at this place.
Digby Harbour-improvements, including repairs and additions to pier, $30,000.

This is to continue the improvements now under way at Digby harbour.
Diligent River Harbour-breakwater-revote of $1,600, lapsed, $7,500.
How much money has been expended at Diligent river, what is it proposed to construct and what is the total cost of the work estimated at?
This is for the construction of a breakwater to make it safe for vessels going in and out of this harbour.
How much has been expended?
Only a small amount- $400.
What is the estimated total cost?
Would the minister state what the dimensions of the wharf are?
360 feet in length, 14 feet wide on top and 30 feet high at the outer end.
Is it the intention of the department to call for tenders and begin operations on this work during the coming year?	.

I cannot say anything beyond this to my Iron, friend, that we are now asking for the amount in the estimates and I have no reason to suppose but what the work will be proceeded with during the coming year. Of course, we have a great many works and we have to get the plans and specifications all ready before we can call for tenders, but I have no reason to suppose that there will be any unnecessary delay in connection with the work.

That answer does not convey very' much meaning to me. I can see that this item is in the estimates, and apparently it is the intention at some time or other to construct this work. But am I to understand that the department say that they will spend $7,500 to construct this wharfs and that after the plans and specifications are brought down they will go ahead and construct it? Surely the department does not do business in that slap-dash sort of fashion. I would like seriously to know if it is the intention of the minister to see that this work is constructed. That is a plain question and I would like to have a plain answer.

The fact of the amount appearing in the estimates is evidence of the intention of the government to proceed with the work. But, before going on with the work, after this appropriation is passed, there will be a very careful survey made by the engineer, plans and specifications will be prepared and in the ordinary course, speaking generally, tenders will be invited. When the tenders come in it may be that the amount will be very considerably higher than what we estimate. I happen to have in my mind a case in my own province last year where an amount was put in the estimates and I expected to go on with a work, but when the tenders came in the amount was considerably higher than the chief engineer estimated and we did not proceed with it. Therefore, I am unable to give my hon. friend the positive assurance that the work will be proceeded with.

I do not profess to be an expert wharf builder but I can say without any hesitation that the department can construct a wharf of splendid quality and of the dimensions mentioned by the minister for the sum placed in the estimates. He need not have the slightest worry about exceeding the amount in the estimates. I find, on looking at the Auditor General's Report for last year V-150, that the sum of $367.77 has already been expended upon this work.
Was that on election day?

Just prior to the election. Am I to understand from the minister that this amount has been expended without any serious intention .on the part of the department to proceed with the work, no plans or specifications having been prepared? The minister is unable to say when this work is to be constructed. He even intimated that if the work cost more than the amount in the appropriation it might not be constructed. It surely is a-most remarkable position for a minister of the Crown to be put in. Could the minister give me an explanation of what this sum was spent for?
My hon. friend has not given me the particulars of the expenditure.
That appears to have been some work done on the Diligent Harbour breakwater. I see there was a foreman and there have evidently been a rock driller, a quarryman and some labourers employed.
I can see that quite as well as the minister can by reading the Auditor General's Report.	.
What does my hon. friend desire me to give him?

I am asking what this sum was expended for and was it expended as a matter of experiment to know whether this wharf should be constructed at a certain point, or was it intended to be a partial sum expended on this wharf which will be completed with the estimate now under consideration?
I cannot tell my hon. friend at this moment but I will look at the engineer's report and give him the information at a later date.

I would like to have the information because it is in my constituency, and if one of my constituents wants to know when the department is going to proceed with this work I want to be able to answer him. That is one of the reasons why I am here. I do not object to the work : indeed I may say it is a very necessary public work. I want to be able to say to my constituents when I go home that this work will be constructed and I feel like pressing the Minister of Public Works to tell me

when he will have it done. There is a very large lumber district around here and large quantities of lumber are shipped, so that the immediate completion of the work is of great interest to Liberals and Conservatives alike.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If every hon. gentleman should demand a similar pledge with respect to the particular work in his constituency the Minister of Public Works might have a larger contract on hand than he could fill. I take it that the presentation of these estimates shows the desire of the minister to carry out the work. If he is asked to say that every one of these works should be commenced at a particular time and carried to completion during the year I certainly should advise him not to give such a pledge.
I would assume that the $367 was for making the testing and boring in the bottom of the harbour which is necessary in all works of this kind in order to estimate the cost.
I do not wish the Minister of Finance for one moment to think that I am unreasonable, but this item has appeared in the estimates at least once before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are quite a number like it.

It is an old friend in the county and I wanted to know whether it was the intention of the minister to complete it in the near future, so that I may be able to tell the shippers in that locality when they will have a wharf on which to land their goods.

The hon. gentleman can tell them what has taken place to-night.
Dover Wharf, $5,000.
Will this be done by tender and contract?
We have not decided.
I thought that all public works were to be done by contract.

I have explained that all work which can be done as economically by contract as by day work will be done by contract. It sometimes happens that the tenders are higher than the estimate of the chief engineer and he recommends that it be done by day labour, or that the work is so remote from the contractors that it can be more economically done the other way.
Dover is not far from Halifax and there is no difficulty in getting contractors.
This Dover is in Guys-boro' county.
I might have supposed that it was not in my county.

There are some publie works to be done in your county.
Dublin Shore-breakwater pier, $10,000.

We expect to finish the work this summer.
Duncan Cove, $6,000.

This is to build an adequate shelter for the lifeboat station, to protect the wharf, and to accommodate fishing boats. The estimated cost is $19,000. This is in the county of Halifax.
Eastern passage harbour, $8,500.

This is also in the county of Halifax. It is for the improvement of the boat harbour which has become almost filled with sand to the great inconvenience of the fishermen. The total probable cost is $13,500.
Will this be done by contract ?
I think this will have to be done by day labour.

This work is badly needed but I think that every working man applying for work there, no matter what his politics, should have a fair show. Of course, there is a lot of favouritism shown and it always will be shown by politicians, but at the same time when a man asks for a day's work he should not be asked what his politics are or to bring a certificate from some party man before he is employed. Men living in the locality should be employed regardless of their political opinions or of anything else ' except that they give a fair day's work for a fair day's pay.

My hon. friend will see how impossible it is for the minister to interfere in these cases. - We endeavour to get a competent foreman, and we leave him free to employ good men in the locality. We give him no instruction about their politics at all. He is expected to use his own judgment and to select men who will give an honest day's work for a fair day's pay.
Fox Island-extension of beach protection work, &c., $1,500.
This is to construct a breakwater. The materials were purchased in 1908-9. This is to complete the work.
Is this to be in the nature of beach protection or the construction of a breakwater?
There is a breakwater there now, which operates, I take it, as a means of protection from the sea. This is merely for an extension of that work.

Last year there was an item for beach protection, if I remember rightly, in the county represented by the Minister of Finance. On ithat occasion the Minister of Public Works justified the work as being necessary to protect certain properties on the water-front which were being more or less carried away from year to year by the action of the water and the tides. At that 'time I drew his attention to the fact that a certain property owned by the Dominion government, and known as Battery Point, at Digby, was becoming from year to year worn away by the action of the tides and the water. Not only was the property diminished in area, but the earth and rocks which were being washed away were being carried into the harbour and forming a very serious sandbar. The minister said he would make a note of my remarks, and he thought some protection would be thrown up in front of the Point to prevent this erosion. Guns owned by the Militia Department are mounted 'there, and I think the property is under the control of the department. I would ask the minister to bear it in mind and provide for it in 'the estimates, if not this year, then next year. It is a very serious detriment to the harbour of Digby.

I will have a note made of it and perhaps confer with the Minister of Militia about it.
Gulf Shore-to complete breakwater between Pugwash and Northport, $1,200.

A year or a year and a half ago the government partly constructed a wharf at the - Gulf Shore in the county of Cumberland. At the same time a survey was taken between Pugwash and Northport. These are two entirely different places. Northport and Pugwash are 18 miles apart.
This is six miles from Pugwash. There was expended on the woTk last year $2,489.95, and the total cost will be $3,700, and this vote is to complete it.

Gulf Shore, Pugwash and Northport would form a triangle. There has been no work other than a survey between Northport and Pugwash, and these points ate 18 miles apart. I would ask the minister to make a memorandum and let me know later if it is -the intention of the department to also construct a wharf between Northport and Pugwash, or if this is only to complete the breakwater at Gulf Shore.

This is to complete the breakwater at Gulf Shore. We have expended $2,489.85, and this amount is asked ito complete the work. The hon. member says that the statement that it is between Pugwash and Northport is an error.
Yes, it was in contemplation at one time tto construct a wharf near Northport.
That is probably how the error has occurred. I would move to amend the item by striking out the words 'between Pugwash and Northport.'
It is no*t the intention to do anything further towards the construction of a wharf between Northport and Pugwash?

We cannot at present, because there is no appropriation.
Habitant River-to lengthen and complete approach to wharf at Canning, $2,000.

The estimated cost of this extension is $25,000. The expenditure to the 31st of March, 1909, was $2,763.17. The expenditure for this year has been $5,256.83 and we are asking for $2,000. That will make $10,000 which will have been expended, and if the further extension is carried on it will take $15,000 more but we are not asking for that now.
That is merely to complete the approach to the wharf at Canning?
Yes.
And the additional $15,000 of which the minister spoke would be required to complete an extension of the wharf, not on the approach.
Yes, that would extend it 750 feet down stream.
Where is this public work?
In the county of Kings.
Represented by the Minister of Militia?	[DOT]

Yes.
Hampton Breakwater-extension-revote of lapsed amount, $3,000.

This is to extend the existing wharf about 100 feet. The object is to prevent the silt and gravel from being washed into the schooner berths which are there alongside the pier. There was a previous vote of $3,000 of which none was used, and we are asking a revote to complete this work.
Harbours, rivers and bridges generally- repairs and improvements, $37,500.
This is the usual general vote, but it is less than last year.

I spoke to the minister with reference to Churchpoint breakwater a few days ago. The minister was kind enough to say then that out of this general vote he would endeavour to provide a berth

on the shoreward end of that wharf which would cost a comparatively insignificant sum, $300 or $400. I would like to have the matter noted now so it may appear as a matter of record.
That is under consideration and if it is decided to proceed with it it can be done out of the general vote.

I would ask the minister to consider the breakwater at Portuguese Cove. They have a very good breakwater there, but it is not as useful as it would be if it had a T across the end. That would make it much more commodious for the people there and would greatly improve the breakwater. I brought the matter to the minister's attention last year and would be glad if he would take it into his consideration with this general vote and could see his way clear to do the work in that way.

It would be an improvement but still it is not an actually necessary work, and I am afraid that the T would cost more than the amount we could take out of the general vote. The general vote is for repairs and small works not exceeding $500. We are providing for a good many wharfs and breakwaters and I did not feel that I could make a special provision for it this year, but I will have it carefully looked into.

What has been the policy in the last few years in purchasing piles for the repairs on existing wharfs and for the construction of new wharfs? Have they been purchased in large quantities for the whole province, or does the department purchase a few here and there in the districts where the work happened to be? Is there any uniformity of price in the purchase of piles?

There has been annually in the maritime provinces an appropriation of a lump sum to purchase creo-soted piling. That piling is purchased in the Southern States, creosoted there and used for various public works. We like to keep a quantity on hand to be used in the construction on wharfs, in the waters affected by the teredo. In harbours into which there is a flow of fresh water the teredo is not nearly so destructive as in harbours not so supplied with fresh water. We endeavour to get it under competition getting prices from the different firms dealing in creosoted timber. There are two large companies in the Southern States which deal in this and we endeavour to buy in fair quantities and at the lowest possible price.

I had not in mind the question of creosoted timber because that cannot be purchased locally. My point was whether there was any policy of pur-32
chasing piling in quantities in order that it might be obtained at a uniform and comparatively reasonable price or if the piling was purchased from different persons in various parts of the province, where work happened to be going on, at any price that the person chose to charge the department, within comparative reason.

We are not in the habit of purchasing ordinary piling in large quantities. We purchase for each particular work. Where we let the work by contract the contractor buys the material himself. If we do the work by day work, we purchase the material for the particular wharf we are proposing to construct. Our engineer or foreman looks around and advises what is best to be done. The piling suitable for one wharf would not do for another. It may depend on the foundation, on the distance before you strike rock, on the rise and fall of the tide, &c., so that we have to buy the piling we require from time to time, and it would not do to buy in large quantities.

I can quite understand that piling varies in size and is purchased at so much per foot. Does the department call for tenders for a certain quantity of piling at so much per foot, or allow the engineer or foreman to go into the locality and do what he thinks best?
It is largely left to the judgment of the engineer to purchase at the lowest market price.
Is this creosote timber purchased direct from the company?
There are two southern companies which supply the timber, and the custom of the department is to keep a fairly large quantity on hand.
It has been brought to my notice that this timber is not purchased from the companies direct, but from a purchasing agent or private individual, who gets the middle man's profit.
Have they agents in every province in Canada?
I think there are two in the lower provinces.
Then the rule of the department is to purchase from the agents of these companies?

Yes, from their authorized agents.
Inverness, Broad Cove Mines-harbour improvements, $10,000.

This is to provide for the carrying on of the proposed works for the accommodation of vessels and to acquire the necessary property from the Inverness Railway and Coal Company. The matter has been under consideration quite a number of years and we have expropriated certain properties from the Inverness Railway and Coal Company. The resident engineer estimates the cost at some $60,000.
Will this complete?

No.
Joggin's Mines-breakwater wharf-repairs and extension, $9,000.

This is to extend the breakwater. The total estimated cost is $9,000.
Judique-approach to breakwater at Mckay's Point, $1,350.

That is the estimated cost to provide for an approach.
Kingsport breakwater pier - extension,

This is to extend the breakwater piers some 200 feet. The present pier is 700 feet long and 40 feet wide, and it is necessary to extend it further to get deeper water and give much needed accommodation to vessels.
Lallave River-to provide for the disposal of saw-dust and other dredged material deposited on foreshore, $4,000.

This is to provide for the removal of dredged material which was deposited at convenient places instead of being carried a good many miles further to the sea.
Lake Ainslie-protected boat channel leading to wharf at Kenlock (Lockbay railway station), $8,000.

This is to give a channel of 15 feet wide and 6 feet at low water at the eastern end of the pier and give access to the wharf.
Leitche's Creek-wharf, $3,500.

This is to afford protection to that wharf. The total cost is estimated at $7,000.
Liscombe Harbour Wharf, $3,000.

That is the estimated total cost.
Litchfield-extension of breakwater, $4,000.

This will be sufficient for the extension of the breakwater.
Little Anse-breakwater, $10,000.

This is to afford protection to fishing vessels. The total cost will be $24,000.
Little River-breakwater-wharf, $4,000.
The total cost will be $10,000. This is to construct a landing pier 165 feet long right out to the depth of 12 feet at low water to afford proper landing and shipping facilities.
Is it intended to call for tenders and give the work by contract?
Yes.
Have thd plans been prepared.
Not the working plans.
I suppose that after the New Year this work will be taken in hand?

Yes, after the Appropriation Act passes. There will be some 45,000 cubic feet of crib-work.
Little Tancook Island-breakwater pier, $5,000. .

This breakwater pier will cost about $18,000. It is to protect the cove formed by a long projection of the southwest part of the island. It is to afford a well sheltered harbour.
Lower Argyle-wharf, $5,000.

There is an old wharf there now almost useless and this is to construct a new one. This is the estimated cost.
McNair's Cove-extension and repairs to breakwater wharf, $6,300.

The total estimated cost is $10,000 but we have expended $3,900 and this will complete.
Main a Dieu-wharf at outer end of eastern breakwater, $10,000.

The total estimated cost is $15,000.
Meteghan-breakwater - renewals and repairs, $4,000.
I move that we amend that item to read ' Meteghan River Breakwater.'

I would be surprised if the minister made that change. There is a place known as Meteghan River wharf, where there is a breakwater, and there is also a place known as Meteghan where there is a public wharf now in a sad state of dilapidation, and which, unless it is speedily protected, will certainly be carried away by storms this winter. I had hoped when I saw this item that it was to be an expenditure at Meteghan where the work is sadly needed. The breakwater at Meteghan, as I have also shown the minister bv means of photographs, is in a bad condition, and unless some repairs are speedily made upon it, it will be damaged if not destroyed. If the minister wishes to amend his estimates by inserting an item for the extension or improvement of the

Meteghan River breakwater, I will have no objection. But where the amount is mentioned in the estimates for Meteghan, which is an entirely different place from Meteghan river, I should object to the change.

The work is very much needed at Meteghan river, and it will take this amount to repair it, while it would take a comparatively small amount to repair the breakwter at Meteghan. This is needed for Meteghan river. But if it is necessary to get a special vote for Meteghan, I will consider that a little later. But I had thought that the repairs there were so comparatively small that they could be done out of the general vote. In the meantime, I ask that this be passed for Meteghan river.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the motion means a diversion of the vote from its original intent, I could not receive it.
It was originally intended for Meteghan river, and it is necessary to alter the reading of the estimate in order definitely to show where the work is to be done.

I have no desire to prevent the expenditure of this sum at Meteghan river. But I have to say with regard to Meteghan that I believe an amount is absolutely necessary to effect the repairs there which are required in the interest, not only of the people who have to use this work, but of the department itself which owns the work. The minister is confusing the breakwater at Meteghan, for which a *comparatively small expenditure is required, with the public landing which is inside that breakwater, and which is an entirely separate structure.
Supposing we voted the money for Meteghan breakwater, it could not be used for a wharf inside the breakwater. We would have to get another vote for that.

As the minister has inserted the word ' breakwater,' meaning a breakwater or a public wharf, I think the amount might be applied to that. But as an amount corresponding to this is necessary for that breakwater and public wharf at Meteghan, I do not think it would be desirable to divert the sum. I do not think the minister would be justified in saying that there could be any possible confusion between the two. I think the work at Meteghan stands in greater need of this expenditure than the work at Meteghan river. The latteT is a comparatively new work, while that at Meteghan is in need of this expenditure to keep it from 'being carried away. If the minister, however, feels that under the circumstances he 32J
could not amend this then providing that a further sum corresponding in amount should be granted for Meteghan, I think would be the most suitable way of meeting the difficulty.

I could not do that, I could not amend these estimates except in-so far as the amount is concerned. As to Meteghan, that is a matter that would be considered later. Suppose that this amount had been allotted to Meteghan breakwater, it could not have been used for the purpose of repairing a wharf at Meteghan, as it is inside the breakwater, while the sum you require for the breakwater at Meteghan is very small, and could be done out of the general vote. There are two Meteghan s, and there is a breakwater at each place. One is known as Meteghan river and the other as Meteghan. Now this was intended for Meteghan river, therefore I would ask the committee to change this to Meteghan river for greater definiteness. If you, Mr. Chairman, feel that you could not make the change, I shall bave to ask you to strike the amount out of the estimates altogether. It is true that my hon. friend spoke to me about the breakwater at Meteghan, and he certainly led me to suppose, whether intentionally or otherwise, that only a small amount would be required to make these repairs.

I do not wish that there should be any misapprehension between the committee or the minister, and myself with regard to this matter. I did state that the expenditure necessary on the Meteghan breakwater would be comparatively trifling, but I also pointed out that the expenditure upon the wharf at Meteghan would be a more serious matter, and I understood from the minister that the matter was receiving attention, and that it would be provided for in the estimates. When I saw this item I concluded that the minister had conceded the necessity and was preparing to meet the emergency. As for his suggestion that if this amendment is not made he will have to move to strike out the item, if that is meant as a mild kind of threat, it does not affect me in the least. I do think that if the minister is unable to allow this item to stand, as it seems to me proper that it should stand, he should be prepared to take the matter of Meteghan breakwater and public landing into immediate consideration because, in the interest of the department over which he presides, repairs are very urgently necessary at a very early date.

I have to tell my hon. friend I would be very glad to do that, but I could not allow an amount which was voted for Meteghan river to go to a breakwater in another place, and I could not allow a single dollar of that to go to the wharf at Meteghan because it is for a

breakwater. Therefore, it would not help my hon. friend, but at the same time I would say that repairs at Meteghan can be met out of the general vote. I will look into the question. If the chairman does not feel that the committee can make this amendment then I shall have to do only what I have power to do and that would be to strike it out altogether.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it appeared that the change was actually a diversion of the vote I would be inclined not to receive the motion, but in so far as it appears to me to be for the purpose of greater definiteness I think I am at liberty to receive the motion.

I therefore beg to move that the word ' river ' be added between the words ' Meteghan ' and ' breakwater.'
Item as amended agreed to.
Middle Island-Port Medway-breakwater- revote of $1,800, lapsed, $2,500.

This is to construct a breakwater on the north side of Middle Island and this is the total estimated cost of the work.
Mira River-wharfs-revote of $700, lapsed, $750.

This is to construct a wharf on the east side of Mira river 3i miles below Victoria bridge. The total estimated cost is $1,160 of which $414 has been expended, leaving what we are asking for to finish the work.
New Harbour-repairs to breakwater at Black Point, $1,000.

This is to repair the breakwater, some fifty feet of which was carried away by a storm. This is the total estimated cost.
Northport-pile wharf-revote of lapsed amount, $3,000.
This is in the county of Cumberland and it is to construct a wharf 200 feet long 30 feet wide and 14 feet high. This will complete the work.
Has any money been expended?*
No, this is probably the one that my hon. friend spoke of.

I think so.
Nyanza Wharf-extension of, &c., $2,500.

This is to extend the wharf fifty feet, using creosoted timber and the object is to enable three vessels to lie at the wharf at the same time. It will provide an increased depth of from eleven to 14 feet of water and the total estimated cost is $2,500.
Where is this?
In Cape Breton at North Victoria.
Perhaps it would not be inadvisable for the minister to say what he means by the word ' &c ' ?

Strike out ' &c Mr. Chairman, if it is objectionable. This is only for the extension. I move that the word ' &c. ' be struck out.
Item, as amended, agreed to.
Owl's Head-to complete wharf, $900.

This is to make provision for the completion of a ballast and crib-work wharf, about 180 feet long, 20 feet wide, for 120 feet from the shore and 30 feet wide for the outer 60 feet. This is to give increased depth of water at the end of the wharf. This will complete it.
Parker's Cove-harbour improvements-revote of $1,600 lapsed, $2,000.

This is to complete the breakwater on the west side of the stream flowing in at Parker's Cove, in order to improve and enlarge the sheltered area for fishing boats and schooners.
Pictou Island-removal of wrecked portion of east, wharf and addition of new sheathed cribwork, &c.-revote of $4,200 lapsed, $6,800.
This will complete the work.

Before the committee rises, there was a statement made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) in connection with an item in the estimates which would give a wrong impression and I desire as a matter of explanation of the merits of the item, to present the facts. He made an attack upon the building of a wharf to accommodate a steamer Of only 10 tons capacity which he said was the capacity of the ' Weymouth.' I have the record of the Department of Marine and Fisheries in which the name of the steamer appears and she is put down as being 102-7 feet long, 19 feet wide 7-6 feet in depth, gross capacity 154 tons, net tonnage 106 tons and 26 horse-power. He made a similar attack upon the new boat. That boat was built after the pattern of the ' Scotia ' and has a tonnage of 350. This is a fair sample of the valuable information that we received from the hon. member from Halifax.

It is necessary for me to give some explanation. I thought the hon. gentleman spoke of the ' Acadia ' which is a very small boat. We do not consider this as anything more than an ordinary boat, a boat that runs along the coast and if we have to build a breakwater at Ingonish costing $30,000 for the accommodation of a boat that might run there once a week or

once a fortnight it is quite a large sum to pay for the service which we would receive. It is a serious matter for us in Nova Scotia where we have a great deal to do with the small amount of money that is spent. We think of our province as the wharf of Canada jutting away out into the Atlantic ocean and therefore we require a great deal. The province of Nova Scotia has done much for the west and for other parts of Canada. There is not a harbour in that province that does not.require some expenditure in the line of providing breakwater accommodation for the fishermen. Therefore, I was anxious that this sum should be divided up amongst some of the other ports. I have no objection at all if the government are willing to spend $30,000 for the accommodation of a very small steamer which will run perhaps not more than once a week or once a fortnight to Ingonish. I think it is not fair to other parts of the province of Nova Scotia which are really in need of breakwaters and wharfs, and which will continue to be in need of them as everybody knows in that part of the country.
